Reduce from six subagents to three by merging related domains to keep the synthesis prompt under 50,000 tokens.
Open with a cross-report key-findings digest before the full reports; add explicit section headers throughout.
explanation: The lost-in-the-middle effect causes attention to drop for content in the middle of long prompts. Two structural interventions counteract this: (1) placing a cross-report digest at the beginning ensures all six reports' critical findings appear in high-attention positions, and (2) explicit section headers create retrieval anchors that improve recall of middle-section content throughout the 95,000-token context. Increasing max_tokens expands output capacity but doesn't redirect attention within the input. Two-pass synthesis breaks cross-report coherence and doubles cost. Reducing from six subagents to three sacrifices research coverage rather than fixing the attention distribution problem.
sourceExcerpt: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. This makes curating what's in context just as important as how much space is available.
sourceHighlight: curating what's in context just as important

text: A customer contacts support and states: 'I have been transferred between three automated systems this week and nothing has been resolved. I am filing a formal complaint and I need to speak with a supervisor immediately—not another bot.' The agent has the customer's full account history and can see the root cause: a billing configuration error fixable with a single API call in approximately 90 seconds. What should the agent do?
options: Immediately escalate to a human supervisor without attempting any actions; honor the explicit escalation request.
Fix the billing error in 90 seconds then escalate with a resolution summary to save the supervisor's time.
Explain the billing fix is straightforward and ask whether the customer prefers resolution or supervisor escalation.
Offer a clear choice between immediate automated resolution or escalation to a human supervisor right now.
explanation: When a customer explicitly states they want a human supervisor—especially after a documented pattern of failed automated escalations—autonomous resolution, even if technically superior, violates the customer's stated authority over the interaction. The exam guide is unambiguous: explicit, emphatic customer requests for human agents must be honored immediately, without first attempting resolution, explanation, or offering alternatives. Options A, C, and D all involve the agent acting or negotiating before honoring the escalation—precisely what the customer is refusing after three prior automated failures.
sourceLabel: Claude Docs: Prompting Best Practices (Autonomy & Safety)
sourceExcerpt: Without guidance, Claude Opus 4.6 may take actions that are difficult to reverse or affect shared systems, such as deleting files, force-pushing, or posting to external services.
sourceHighlight: difficult to reverse or affect shared systems

text: An agent spent 6 hours analyzing a legacy monolith, documenting 340 classes across 18 service boundaries with specific method signatures, coupling relationships, and migration risks. By hour 5, responses cited exact class names and file paths accurately. By hour 6, the agent describes services as 'the data access layer' and 'the authentication service' without citing specific classes. The engineering team needs the specific findings for a 3-month migration plan, and the session context is near capacity. What approach correctly addresses both context degradation and preservation of detailed findings?
options: Run /compact to compress the context history and continue the session with a reduced token footprint.
Before context exhaustion, write structured discovery files to disk—one per service boundary with specific classes.
Start a completely fresh analysis session focused only on the 18 service boundaries to regenerate all findings.
Extract a partial summary covering the still-accurate hour-5 findings and build the migration plan from that subset.
explanation: Scratchpad files solve both problems simultaneously: specific findings are externalized to disk before context fills, making them immune to compression and dilution, and the agent can reference these files explicitly in subsequent queries to retrieve exact class names and signatures rather than reconstructing from degraded context. Running /compact compresses history into a lossy summary—it reduces token usage but destroys the specificity of class names and method signatures. Starting a completely fresh session discards 6 hours of work and may surface different findings on a second pass. Extracting a partial summary produces lossy output for the already-degraded portions and risks missing information that should have been externalized earlier.
sourceExcerpt: Compaction automatically summarizes earlier parts of the conversation on the server, so the conversation can continue past the context window limit.
sourceHighlight: automatically summarizes earlier parts of the conversation

text: A developer asks Claude Code: 'Migrate the legacy auth module to support OAuth 2.1 with full backward compatibility for 6,000 existing sessions using the legacy token format.' The module has 23 classes with undocumented session lifecycle handling, token refresh logic spread across 7 files, 3 undocumented behavioral quirks affecting mobile clients, and zero test coverage. The developer has no prior knowledge of the module internals. Which decomposition strategy is most appropriate?
options: Fixed sequential decomposition: audit all 23 classes, write tests, implement OAuth 2.1, then validate compatibility.
Parallel subagent analysis assigning one subagent per class to document behavior simultaneously, then aggregate.
Dynamic adaptive decomposition: explore the module first, map session and token flows, then adapt plan as needed.
Apply the standard OAuth 2.1 migration pattern since the protocol is well-documented and adapting is straightforward.
explanation: This task has unknown complexity in multiple dimensions: undocumented quirks, cross-file token logic, mobile-specific edge cases, and an undefined test baseline. A fixed sequence (A) fails when undocumented quirks invalidate earlier steps. Parallel class-per-subagent analysis (B) produces class-level findings but misses cross-class session lifecycle flows and emergent behaviors distributed across 7 files. Standard pattern application (D) applies generic knowledge without adapting to specific undocumented behaviors—the cause of most migration regressions. Dynamic adaptive decomposition correctly treats this as an open-ended investigation: explore first, discover constraints, then plan and adapt.
sourceExcerpt: Whereas it's topographically similar, the key difference from parallelization is its flexibility—subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input.
sourceHighlight: subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator

text: Pallisade Data runs a four-stage data pipeline: an intake agent, an enrichment agent, a validation agent, and a reporting agent, each connected to the same MCP server. For deployment simplicity, the platform team wired all four agents to the identical connection, so every agent can call all 22 tools spanning all four stages, even though each agent's job only touches its own stage. In production, the validation agent has started calling enrichment-only tools mid-validation to 'double-check' fields that were already enriched upstream, adding unnecessary API cost and, twice now, overwriting entries in the enrichment cache that validation was never meant to write to. A system-prompt rule telling the validation agent not to touch enrichment tools was tried first but proved unreliable once the pipeline was under real load. What is the most effective structural fix?
options: Add a system-prompt rule instructing the validation agent never to call enrichment tools, and monitor for violations.
Add a PostToolUse hook that automatically reverts any enrichment-cache writes made by the validation agent.
Require every enrichment tool call to include a written justification string before it is allowed to execute.
Scope each agent's available tools to only what its own pipeline stage requires, removing enrichment tools from the validation agent's toolset entirely.
explanation: Scoping each agent's tools to its own pipeline stage removes the enrichment tools from the validation agent's toolset entirely, so the cross-role calls literally cannot happen -- a structural guarantee rather than a probabilistic one. A system-prompt rule is instructional: it worked initially but degraded under load exactly as described, because the model can still reach tools that remain technically available. A PostToolUse hook that reverts bad writes only cleans up after the mistake already happened, including the unnecessary API cost. Requiring a justification string still lets the call proceed once the agent supplies some text, and doesn't remove a capability that shouldn't exist in this role at all. The reliable fix is always to shrink what's actually reachable, not to add checks around tools that shouldn't be exposed in the first place.
sourceExcerpt: Consolidate related operations into fewer tools. Rather than creating a separate tool for every action (`create_pr`, `review_pr`, `merge_pr`), group them into a single tool with an `action` parameter. Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity and make your tool surface easier for Claude to navigate.
sourceHighlight: Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity

text: At Quillfeather Data Co, an engineer asked Claude Code to implement a function that validates and normalizes international phone numbers before they're stored, giving only the instructions 'handle all formats correctly' and 'be thorough about edge cases.' The result handles common US-style numbers fine, but silently mishandles numbers with a leading +44 country code, numbers written with extension suffixes like 'x204', and numbers submitted with no country code at all, defaulting them all to a guess instead of flagging them. The engineer restated the same 'be thorough' instruction more forcefully, with no improvement in the actual output. Two days remain before this ships to production, and the engineer wants a way to make real, checkable progress on exactly these three known gaps rather than continuing to restate the same general request. What should the engineer do next?
options: Repeat the same 'handle all formats correctly, be thorough' instruction a second time so the model reconsiders more carefully.
Ask Claude to regenerate the entire function from scratch using a larger, more capable model instead of iterating on the current one.
Write a failing unit test for each specific format the current implementation mishandles, then have Claude iterate until each test passes.
Add a long prose paragraph to CLAUDE.md describing every phone number format the function must someday support.
explanation: Writing one failing unit test per known gap -- a +44-prefixed number, a number with an extension suffix, a number missing a country code -- turns three vague, previously-unaddressed cases into a concrete, checkable target: Claude can run the tests, see exactly which ones fail and why, and iterate until each passes, giving both engineer and model a verifiable definition of done. Repeating the same 'be thorough' wording (option A) already failed once and gives the model no new information to act on. Regenerating the whole function with a bigger model (option B) discards a mostly-working implementation to chase a problem that isn't about model capability. A long prose CLAUDE.md paragraph enumerating formats (option D) is still an unverifiable specification in words, the same category of instruction that already didn't work.
sourceExcerpt: Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare. It's the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from.
sourceHighlight: Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare

text: A contract analysis pipeline extracts 18 fields from regulatory filings. The 'governing_law_jurisdiction' field has been retried 8 times across three different prompt phrasings and returns null each time. Validation logs confirm the field is required. Manual review of the submitted document reveals the governing law is established by reference: 'This agreement shall be governed pursuant to the Master Services Agreement dated March 2019'—and the 2019 MSA was not included in the provided document set. What is the correct system response?
options: Retry the extraction using a more capable model, since the current model cannot resolve cross-document references.
Halt retries—the data is in a missing document. Record null with provenance, flag for human review, continue pipeline.
Add few-shot examples showing cross-reference resolution so the model learns to infer jurisdiction from citations.
Mark the governing_law_jurisdiction field optional in the schema, since some contracts define jurisdiction by reference.
explanation: Eight consistent null results with confirmed source document absence is a diagnostic signal: this is a missing-data problem, not a model capability problem. Retries are effective for format errors, schema mismatches, and ambiguous prompts—not for information that simply isn't in the provided document. The correct response is to halt retries, record null with full provenance identifying the referenced document, flag for human review to obtain the MSA, and continue the pipeline. A more capable model cannot extract information absent from its context. Few-shot examples on cross-reference patterns teach extraction from references that are present—this jurisdiction isn't present in any form. Making the field optional silently accepts the null without surfacing the missing document dependency.
sourceLabel: Anthropic Engineering: Writing Tools for Agents
sourceExcerpt: If a tool call raises an error (for example, during input validation), you can prompt-engineer your error responses to clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements.
sourceHighlight: prompt-engineer your error responses

text: A competitive intelligence analyst asks a synthesis agent to produce one market-adoption figure for an executive briefing on AI coding assistants. The agent pulls three credible-looking sources: a 2023 Gartner survey of 2,800 enterprises reporting 42% production deployment, the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey of 89,000 developers across all types reporting 71% usage, and a 2024 study commissioned by an AI vendor surveying 400 of its own customers reporting 94% adoption. Each figure comes from a different population and methodology, and none of them measured quite the same thing. The analyst just wants a single number for the briefing slide, but the agent has to decide how to responsibly synthesize three figures that disagree. What should the synthesis agent report?
options: Report only Source A's 42% figure as most credible, treating Gartner as the highest-authority enterprise research firm.
Compute a single weighted-average adoption figure, adjusting each source's weight by its reported sample size.
Present all three figures with full source attribution, annotating incomparability and flagging Source C as vendor-biased.
Report only Sources A and B with attribution, discarding Source C entirely as vendor-commissioned and unreliable.
explanation: When credible sources produce different figures due to different populations and methodologies, the synthesis agent's role is attribution and disambiguation—not selection or blending. All three numbers are accurate within their own sampling frames; the spread reflects genuine population differences, not measurement error. Selecting only Source A's figure presents enterprise deployments as the whole market. Computing a weighted average produces a meaningless composite that destroys the population-variation information. Discarding Source C entirely makes an editorial selection the agent is not positioned to make—vendor-customer data is useful for specific audiences and belongs in the attribution. Transparent attribution lets executives choose the relevant population for their context.
sourceExcerpt: All prompting techniques — from clarity and examples to XML structuring, role prompting, thinking, and prompt chaining — are covered in Prompting best practices. That's the living reference; start there.
sourceHighlight: role prompting, thinking, and prompt chaining

text: A financial services agent processes customer refund requests. The system prompt states: 'Refunds above $500 require a compliance review ticket before processing.' Post-audit analysis shows 4.2% of refunds above $500 are processed without a compliance ticket—specifically when customers split refund discussions across multiple turns ('First, I'd like $200 back for the service fee... and also $350 for the hardware...'). Three rounds of system prompt revisions have each reduced but not eliminated the failure rate. The compliance team requires 0% violations for regulatory reasons. What is the correct architectural fix?
options: Add a dedicated compliance validation agent that reviews every refund request before the main agent can process it.
Add server-side validation in the refund API that rejects requests once the cumulative session total passes $500.
Use a PostToolUse hook that detects violations and automatically rolls back non-compliant transactions afterward.
Implement a PreToolUse hook that intercepts each refund call, computes cumulative session total, and blocks if over limit.
explanation: Three prompt revisions that reduce but cannot eliminate violations confirm that probabilistic prompt-based compliance cannot satisfy the 0% regulatory requirement. PreToolUse hooks provide deterministic pre-execution enforcement: the hook executes at the SDK layer before the tool call reaches the server, with full access to tool parameters and cumulative session state for multi-turn amount tracking. This cannot be bypassed by any prompt interpretation path. A dedicated validation agent has the same probabilistic limitations as the system prompt. Server-side validation in the refund API catches the error after the tool call is issued and requires a retry cycle rather than seamless workflow redirection. A PostToolUse hook with rollback processes the refund first—a compliance failure has already occurred, and rollback may not be complete or instantaneous.
sourceExcerpt: PreToolUse: Before a tool call executes. Can block it. PostToolUse: After a tool call succeeds.
sourceHighlight: Before a tool call executes. Can block it

text: At Halcyon Fintech, the payments team must migrate a core payments library used across 45 files spanning the checkout service, the refund pipeline, and three internal admin tools. Two viable migration approaches have emerged in team discussion: building an adapter shim that preserves the old interface while routing to new internals, versus rewriting every call site directly to the new API. These two approaches carry meaningfully different infrastructure implications — the shim adds a translation layer that must be maintained and eventually retired, while the direct rewrite touches production payment code across dozens of files in one pass with no fallback layer. The engineering lead knows that picking the wrong approach after files are already being edited would be expensive to unwind given the scope and the sensitivity of payments code. Before any file is touched, which review architecture should the lead select first to decide between the shim and the rewrite?
options: Plan mode — have Claude explore the codebase, weigh the adapter-shim and rewrite approaches, and propose a plan before any file is changed.
Direct execution — begin rewriting call sites across all 45 files immediately, since any individual file can always be reverted later if wrong.
A single-phase workflow that runs the adapter-shim and rewrite approaches in parallel subagents, then merges whichever finishes first.
Skip any review architecture entirely and rely on the hooks system to catch and block invalid edits after they have already been made.
explanation: Plan mode exists precisely for this scenario: large-scale changes with multiple valid approaches and architectural implications, where committing to the wrong one is costly to unwind across 45 files. Direct execution is appropriate for well-scoped single-file changes, not open architectural decisions. Running both approaches in parallel wastes effort on a decision that should be made once, deliberately. Hooks enforce rules on tool calls; they don't help choose between architectural approaches.
sourceExcerpt: Plan mode tells Claude to research and propose changes without making them. Claude reads files, runs shell commands to explore, and writes a plan, but does not edit your source.
sourceHighlight: writes a plan, but does not edit your source

text: It's the last day of the fiscal quarter at Ashenvale Capital, and a contractor is racing to finish a batch of migration scripts against the trading-data warehouse before a hard cutoff. He proposes running Claude Code overnight with --dangerously-skip-permissions so it can work through the whole batch without stopping for approval on every file write or database command, arguing the team is 'just trying to move fast under a deadline' and that policy concerns can be sorted out later. The risk officer flags the request and asks the team to articulate, precisely, what technical risk this introduces -- not just that it violates policy. What is the real risk being introduced by running unattended with all permission checks disabled?
options: There's no meaningful risk difference, since Claude would ask for confirmation before anything destructive even in this bypass mode.
The main risk is that skipping permission prompts removes any check on unattended destructive actions Claude might take against production data.
The main risk is purely a policy compliance issue with no realistic technical risk to the production trading-data warehouse itself.
The main risk is slower throughput, since permission prompts actually make batch migrations complete faster by parallelizing approvals.
explanation: Skipping permission prompts removes the one point at which a human would normally see and approve a risky or destructive action before it runs against the warehouse -- under deadline pressure with a large unattended batch, that means Claude could alter or delete production trading data with no check in the loop, not merely that a policy document gets violated. The safer way to move quickly without a prompt on every action is deterministic, narrow permission through hooks or --allowedTools scoped to only the specific safe actions the migration actually needs, rather than disabling every check at once. Claiming no risk difference exists (option A) ignores what the bypass flag specifically disables. Framing it as purely a compliance issue with no technical risk (option C) understates what an unattended, unchecked destructive action can do. Prompts do not parallelize approvals or speed up throughput (option D).
sourceExcerpt: Hooks are user-defined shell commands that execute at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle. They provide deterministic control over Claude Code's behavior, ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them.
sourceHighlight: ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them

text: A policy team at a fintech startup asks Claude to research three independent regulatory frameworks—GDPR, CCPA, and the incoming EU AI Act—that could affect an upcoming product launch. Each framework can be researched independently and in parallel, but before the findings go anywhere they need to be cross-verified against each other, since the frameworks sometimes impose conflicting requirements. The final report goes to external legal counsel and regulators, so a human compliance officer must review and approve it before anything is published. The team is choosing which Claude Code architecture supports parallel research, cross-verification, and a mandatory approval gate all in one workflow. Which architecture fits this task?
options: Direct execution across all three regulatory frameworks at once, since each research subtask is independent and needs no upfront planning or coordination.
Plan mode only, since Claude will "plan" out the research approach for all three regulatory frameworks before running any part of it.
A multi-phase workflow: parallel research agents, then a verification/synthesis pass, then a human approval checkpoint before the report is released.
A single long-running agent session with no intermediate checkpoints at all, since checkpoints only ever slow down the research process.
explanation: This task has three properties that call for a structured multi-phase workflow: parallelizable subtasks, a need for cross-verification, and a mandatory human approval gate before an external-facing artifact ships. Plan mode only covers pre-execution planning, not the verification and approval phases. Direct execution has no mechanism for the fan-out/verify/gate structure. A single unchecked session removes the human checkpoint the scenario explicitly requires.
sourceExcerpt: Agents can then pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers. It's also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control.
sourceHighlight: pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers

text: At Solstice Bank, the data platform team is preparing a database schema migration that touches a table holding customer financial transaction records. Regulatory policy requires explicit compliance sign-off before any change to this table can run in production, and the compliance officer has made clear that verbal or after-the-fact approval does not satisfy the audit requirement. The migration itself is moderate in scope, touching 12 files across the schema definitions, ORM models, and migration scripts, but the risk profile is high because an unreviewed mistake could corrupt financial records subject to regulatory audit. The team lead is choosing how to structure the work so that a human compliance reviewer sees and approves the exact plan before a single line of the migration executes against production data. What is the most appropriate review architecture for this situation?
options: Direct execution, since 12 files is a moderate and well-understood scope.
A fully autonomous multi-phase workflow that runs the migration and rolls back automatically if compliance tests fail after the fact.
Skip planning and rely on a PostToolUse hook to detect compliance violations after the migration has already run.
Plan mode to propose the migration, with execution gated behind explicit human approval of that plan given the compliance risk.
explanation: Risk level, not just file count, should drive the choice here: even a moderate-scope change warrants plan mode when the blast radius includes compliance-sensitive financial data and explicit sign-off is required before execution. Direct execution skips the human checkpoint the scenario demands. An autonomous rollback-on-failure workflow still lets the risky change execute before catching problems. A PostToolUse hook only reacts after the migration already ran — too late for a pre-execution compliance gate.
sourceExcerpt: Plan mode tells Claude to research and propose changes without making them. Claude reads files, runs shell commands to explore, and writes a plan, but does not edit your source.
sourceHighlight: writes a plan, but does not edit your source

text: A data engineer asks Claude to normalize a spreadsheet of informal, hand-entered address strings—things like "123 Main St Apt 4b" and "123 main street, unit 4-B"—into a single fixed schema of street, unit, city, and postal code fields. Each time the engineer reruns the same prose instruction asking for a "normalized" address, Claude applies a different, inconsistent interpretation of which parts belong in which field and how abbreviations should be expanded. The engineer has already tried rephrasing the instruction more forcefully, with no improvement in consistency. What is the most effective next step to get consistent, correct normalization?
options: Provide 2-3 concrete input/output example pairs showing the exact transformation you expect.
Repeat the same prose instruction more emphatically, adding words like "always" and "consistently."
Lower the temperature to zero so the same prompt produces the same output every time.
Split the instruction into ten separate short sentences instead of one paragraph.
explanation: Concrete input/output examples are the most reliable way to communicate an exact transformation when prose descriptions are being interpreted inconsistently — they remove ambiguity about what "normalized" means in practice. Rewording the same prose more forcefully doesn't resolve the underlying ambiguity. Lowering temperature improves determinism for a given interpretation but doesn't fix which interpretation is chosen. Reformatting the same ambiguous instruction into shorter sentences doesn't add the missing information.
sourceExcerpt: Few well-crafted examples (known as few-shot or multishot prompting) improve accuracy and consistency. Effective examples should be relevant (mirroring your actual use case closely) and diverse (covering edge cases).
sourceHighlight: improve accuracy and consistency

text: A platform team asks Claude to implement a caching layer with a specific LRU-with-TTL eviction policy that must behave correctly even when multiple threads read from and write to the cache concurrently. Early attempts compile and pass a quick manual smoke test, but the team suspects subtle eviction-ordering bugs will only surface under concurrent access and edge cases like simultaneous expiration and eviction. Adding more prose description of the desired behavior across follow-up messages hasn't reliably closed the gap. The team wants an iteration approach that gives Claude a concrete, checkable signal rather than relying on subjective judgment calls. What is the most effective way to guide iterative improvement toward correct behavior?
options: Describe the eviction policy in increasingly detailed prose across several follow-up messages, adding nuance each time.
Write a test suite covering expected behavior and edge cases first, then iterate by sharing the specific test failures with Claude.
Ask Claude to self-review its own caching implementation for correctness before ever presenting the result back to you.
Ask Claude to write the caching layer three separate ways and simply pick whichever implementation looks the cleanest.
explanation: Test-driven iteration gives Claude a concrete, checkable signal — examining existing test files and matching expected behavior lets a pass/fail check drive convergence instead of relying on subjective prose descriptions. Detailed prose alone still leaves interpretation ambiguous for concurrency edge cases. Self-review suffers from the same self-assessment blind spot as any self-review without an independent check. Picking the "cleanest" of three variants has no correctness signal at all.
sourceExcerpt: Claude examines your existing test files to match the style, frameworks, and assertion patterns already in use. Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare.
sourceHighlight: examines your existing test files to match the style, frameworks, and assertion patterns

text: Priya is reviewing a pull request from a teammate that touches the processBatch function in the billing service. In a single pass she finds four things: an off-by-one error in the loop bound, a race condition that surfaces only because of that off-by-one when two workers process the same batch window, a variable named tmp2 that obscures what it actually holds, and, in a completely unrelated file, a missing null check on a config loader that has nothing to do with processBatch. She wants to hand these findings to Claude Code to fix, but she's worried that dumping everything into one flat message will cause Claude to patch the race condition without properly accounting for the off-by-one it depends on, while also risking that the naming and null-check fixes get tangled up with the more delicate concurrency change. How should Priya structure her feedback to Claude across her messages?
options: Report all four issues together as one single flat, completely undifferentiated list, and let Claude decide entirely on its own which order to fix them in.
Always fix every single issue together in one combined message regardless of whether the issues actually interact with each other, purely to save extra round trips.
Provide the off-by-one error and the race condition together in one detailed message since they interact, and address the unrelated variable-naming and null-check issues separately.
Always fix issues one at a time in complete isolation, regardless of whether they actually interact with each other in the code, to avoid confusing Claude.
explanation: The right granularity depends on interaction: issues that interact (the off-by-one and the race condition it feeds into) are best described together in one detailed pass — similar to a self-correction chain where each pass has a clear, scoped criterion — while independent issues (naming, an unrelated null check) are better handled separately so a fix for one doesn't get conflated with unrelated changes. A flat undifferentiated list risks Claude fixing the race condition without accounting for the off-by-one it depends on. Always batching or always separating ignores whether the issues actually interact.
sourceExcerpt: The most common chaining pattern is self-correction: generate a draft, have Claude review it against criteria, then have Claude refine based on the review, with each step being a separate API call so you can log, evaluate, or branch at any point.
sourceHighlight: each step being a separate API call so you can log, evaluate, or branch

text: Copperline Cloud Systems runs an unattended nightly claude -p job that reviews every open pull request's diff and reports findings to a compliance dashboard. Two hard requirements apply: the dashboard's ingestion code validates each finding against a strict JSON Schema (fields: file, line, severity, message) and rejects anything that doesn't conform outright, and finance separately wants per-invocation cost tracked automatically so a monthly spend report can be generated without any extra instrumentation work. The job must also never modify any file in the repository it's reviewing, since it runs with no engineer present to catch a mistake. An earlier proof of concept that asked Claude to 'output your findings as JSON' in the prompt text produced output that mostly, but not always, matched the required field names, breaking the dashboard's ingestion on the invocations that didn't conform. The platform engineer needs a single configuration that reliably satisfies the schema requirement, the cost-tracking requirement, and the read-only requirement all at once. Which configuration does that?
options: Run with -p and --output-format json only, then have a separate script infer field names heuristically from the free-form structured output.
Run with -p, --output-format text, and parse the dashboard fields out of the prose using regular expressions maintained by the platform team.
Run interactively so an engineer can manually reformat each finding into the dashboard's required schema before it's forwarded downstream.
Run with -p, --output-format json combined with --json-schema defining the required fields, restricting tools to read-only for the unattended job.
explanation: Running with -p for non-interactive execution, --output-format json combined with --json-schema defining the exact required fields, and tool access restricted to read-only satisfies all three requirements together: --json-schema guarantees the structured output actually conforms to the dashboard's schema rather than merely resembling it, --output-format json's response payload already carries per-invocation cost data for the finance report with no extra instrumentation, and restricting tools to read-only guarantees the job cannot modify the repository it's reviewing. Inferring field names heuristically from free-form output (option A) reintroduces the same unreliable-conformance problem the proof of concept already hit. Regex-parsing prose output (option B) is exactly the fragile approach that broke before. Interactive execution (option C) defeats the purpose of an unattended nightly job entirely.
sourceLabel: Claude Code Docs: Headless Mode (Structured Output)
sourceExcerpt: To get output conforming to a specific schema, use --output-format json with --json-schema and a JSON Schema definition. The response includes metadata about the request (session ID, usage, etc.) with the structured output in the structured_output field.
sourceHighlight: use --output-format json with --json-schema and a JSON Schema definition

text: Wexford Telecom's security team has one absolute requirement: no Claude Code session, for any engineer, on any project, should ever read or print the contents of files under secrets/ -- not even to help debug an issue, and not even if an engineer's own prompt asks for it directly. The rule 'Never read files under secrets/' has been written into the shared project CLAUDE.md for months. During an urgent outage last week, a contractor's session read and quoted back part of a file under secrets/ anyway, after the contractor had pasted a long block of unrelated log output into the same message -- the CLAUDE.md instruction was technically still present, but got outweighed amid everything else in that prompt. Security wants a fix that makes this outcome structurally impossible for every engineer, not one that depends on the instruction winning the model's attention every time. What should they implement?
options: Configure permissions.deny for the secrets/ path in settings, since settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides.
Move the 'never read secrets/' line from the project CLAUDE.md into every engineer's personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file instead.
Rewrite the instruction in CLAUDE.md using stronger language, such as prefixing it with 'ABSOLUTE RULE' in bold capital letters.
Ask each engineer to manually confirm they haven't pasted anything that would cause Claude to read the secrets/ directory.
explanation: Configuring permissions.deny for the secrets/ path at the settings level is enforced by the client itself, independent of anything in the current prompt or how much competing text surrounds the instruction -- it isn't a matter of the model weighing instructions at all. Moving the same instruction into each engineer's personal CLAUDE.md (option B) keeps it as advisory text with the same failure mode, just relocated. Rewriting it in bold capitals as an 'ABSOLUTE RULE' (option C) is still advisory phrasing competing for attention in a crowded prompt, exactly what failed during the outage. Relying on each engineer to manually self-police what they paste (option D) depends on human diligence under pressure, the same condition that caused the original incident.
sourceLabel: Claude Code Docs: Memory (Managing CLAUDE.md for Teams)
sourceExcerpt: Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides to do. CLAUDE.md instructions shape Claude's behavior but are not a hard enforcement layer.
sourceHighlight: Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides to do

text: Deepa built a /security-review slash-command skill that scans pull requests for injection vulnerabilities, hardcoded secrets, and unsafe deserialization. She wants the skill to only ever read files -- never write, edit, or execute shell commands -- even when it's invoked by a senior engineer whose personal Claude Code settings normally grant broad Bash and Edit permissions. During a recent test run, a developer with elevated personal permissions triggered /security-review, and while investigating a suspicious dependency Claude nearly ran a shell command to patch the flagged file directly. Deepa needs a mechanism that constrains the skill's own capabilities regardless of what the invoking developer's account is otherwise allowed to do elsewhere. How should she enforce this at the skill level?
options: Add a warning in the skill's description telling Claude not to edit or execute anything.
Set allowed-tools in the skill's frontmatter to the read-only tool set the skill needs.
Require the developer to manually deny edit permissions in their personal settings before running the skill.
Rely on the model's general judgment that security reviews shouldn't modify code.
explanation: The allowed-tools frontmatter field scopes exactly which tools are available while a skill is active — a configuration-level restriction rather than a hope that the model behaves — and it holds regardless of the invoking developer's broader permissions. A prose warning is a probabilistic constraint, not an enforced one. Requiring per-developer manual configuration is fragile and easy to forget. Relying on general judgment provides no guarantee at all.
sourceExcerpt: Set to fork to run in a forked subagent context. allowed-tools: Tools Claude can use without asking permission when this skill is active. argument-hint: Hint shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments.
sourceHighlight: Set to fork to run in a forked subagent context

text: After a Claude Code session accidentally deleted a shared logs/ directory outside its intended scratch space during a cleanup task, the platform team at Vantage Analytics wants a guarantee that this can never happen again across any engineer's session, in any project, company-wide. They had already added a CLAUDE.md note asking Claude to confine rm -rf to /tmp/scratch, but the incident happened despite that guidance already being in place. The team needs the restriction to hold even if a future prompt is unusual, a session's CLAUDE.md is missing, or a developer simply forgets to mention the scratch directory -- it must be enforced regardless of what Claude decides to do, not merely suggested to it. Which configuration mechanism should they use to structurally prevent rm -rf from ever touching a path outside the designated scratch directory?
options: A project-level CLAUDE.md instruction that tells Claude never to run destructive commands outside the scratch directory.
A Skill with an argument-hint that reminds the invoking developer to double-check any destructive commands first.
A PreToolUse hook that inspects Bash calls and blocks the command before execution if it doesn't match the allowed pattern.
A .claude/rules/ file scoped to shell-script paths that documents safe deletion practices for developers to follow.
explanation: Hooks provide deterministic control over Claude Code's behavior, ensuring certain actions always happen (or are always blocked) rather than depending on the model choosing to comply — exactly what "structurally prevented" requires. CLAUDE.md instructions, argument-hint text, and rules files are all prompt-level guidance a model could fail to follow under an unusual input; none of them can guarantee the command never executes.
sourceExcerpt: Hooks are user-defined shell commands that execute at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle. They provide deterministic control over Claude Code's behavior, ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them.
sourceHighlight: deterministic control over Claude Code's behavior

text: The release engineering team at Fenwick Systems wants a standardized way to generate the changelog whenever someone cuts a new release -- pulling merged PR titles since the last tag, categorizing them by type, and formatting them to match the existing CHANGELOG.md style. This should only run when a release manager deliberately kicks it off during a release, not automatically during ordinary day-to-day coding sessions, and it shouldn't fire every time someone edits an unrelated file. The team has already ruled out anything that runs on every session or every edit, since that would be far noisier than what they actually need. Which configuration mechanism best fits a workflow that is invoked deliberately, on demand, only when someone is actually cutting a release?
options: A project-level CLAUDE.md entry describing the changelog format, since CLAUDE.md is always loaded into every session.
A .claude/rules/ file scoped with a glob pattern that specifically matches changelog files whenever they are edited.
A PostToolUse hook that automatically regenerates the changelog file after every single file edit is made.
A project-scoped skill in .claude/skills/, since skills are invoked on demand rather than always-loaded.
explanation: Skills are the right mechanism for task-specific workflows invoked on demand — CLAUDE.md is for universal standards that should apply to every session, the opposite of "invoked deliberately" here. A glob-scoped rules file is for conventions tied to editing specific file types, not an on-demand release procedure. A hook firing after every edit would run far more often than intended, not just when cutting a release.
sourceExcerpt: Set to fork to run in a forked subagent context. allowed-tools: Tools Claude can use without asking permission when this skill is active. argument-hint: Hint shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments.
sourceHighlight: Set to fork to run in a forked subagent context

text: At Ridgeline Software, test files like user.test.ts and payment.test.py live directly beside the source files they cover, scattered across dozens of directories in the monorepo rather than collected under one tests/ folder. The QA lead wants one consistent set of conventions -- a fixed assertion style, no live network calls, required teardown blocks -- applied automatically any time Claude edits a test file, no matter which directory it happens to sit in. She doesn't want to place a CLAUDE.md file in every directory that happens to contain tests, since new test files show up in new directories almost every week, and she doesn't want engineers to have to remember to invoke anything manually before editing a test. What's the most maintainable configuration mechanism for making the testing conventions load automatically based on file pattern rather than directory location?
options: A .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter specifying a glob pattern like paths: ["**/*.test.*"].
A CLAUDE.md file placed in every subdirectory that happens to contain test files.
A single monolithic root CLAUDE.md with a section for testing, relying on Claude to infer when it applies.
A skill that a developer must manually invoke before editing any test file.
explanation: Path-scoped rules using YAML frontmatter with a paths glob load automatically whenever Claude is working with matching files, independent of directory location — exactly what scattered test files require. Directory-bound CLAUDE.md files can't easily cover files spread across many directories. A monolithic root file relies on inference rather than deterministic matching. A manually invoked skill isn't automatic.
sourceExcerpt: Rules can be scoped to specific files using YAML frontmatter with the paths field. These conditional rules only apply when Claude is working with files matching the specified patterns.
sourceHighlight: scoped to specific files using YAML frontmatter with the paths field

text: Following an incident in which a Claude Code session at Castleton Financial ran curl against an unapproved external endpoint while debugging a webhook integration, the security team wants a hard, non-negotiable rule: no session, in any project, under any personal or project CLAUDE.md configuration, may ever invoke the Bash tool with curl against a host outside the approved allowlist. They know individual engineers control their own personal CLAUDE.md files and project maintainers control their own project-level files, and they don't trust either layer to reliably carry a restriction this critical, since either one could be edited, forgotten, or overridden. They need the rule to apply above and independently of whatever any project or personal configuration happens to say. Where should this restriction live?
options: In every project's root CLAUDE.md file, instructing Claude in plain language never to invoke curl against any external host under any circumstance.
In managed/organization-level settings permission rules that deny the pattern outright, layered above any project or personal configuration.
In each developer's personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file, so the restriction automatically travels with them across every project they touch.
In a .claude/rules/ file scoped by a glob pattern to any file that happens to contain the literal word "curl" somewhere in its contents.
explanation: Permission rules in settings can pre-approve or block specific tools and are layered on top of, and enforced independently of, whatever a project's or user's CLAUDE.md says — making them the correct place for a non-negotiable, organization-wide deny rule. CLAUDE.md-based approaches are prompt-level instructions a session could still deviate from, and neither is organization-scoped by design. A rules file scoped by file content doesn't govern tool invocation at all.
sourceExcerpt: Modes set the baseline. Layer permission rules on top to pre-approve or block specific tools.
sourceHighlight: Layer permission rules on top to pre-approve or block specific tools

text: Windermere Retail's internal research tool lets merchandising analysts type free-form ad hoc requests like 'how are our top 3 competitors pricing seasonal outdoor furniture this quarter' or, on a different day, 'what packaging changes have all 7 major snack brands made in the last year.' The number of competitors, sub-questions, and comparison axes varies wildly request to request and can't be predetermined by the engineering team building the system; some requests decompose cleanly into 2 parallel lookups, others need 6 or more. The team is deciding between a fixed four-stage prompt chain (identify subject, gather data, compare, summarize) versus an architecture where a lead LLM call decides, per request, how many worker subtasks are needed and dispatches accordingly before combining the results itself. Which architecture actually fits Windermere's requirement that subtask count and shape can't be fixed in advance?
options: A fixed four-stage prompt chain, since chaining always outperforms dynamic decomposition regardless of how variable the underlying task is.
A routing architecture where a classifier picks exactly one specialized downstream path per request and no parallel workers are used.
An orchestrator-workers architecture, where a central LLM dynamically breaks down each request, delegates to workers, and synthesizes the results.
A single long-context agent that reads through all competitor data linearly in one continuous pass without ever delegating subtasks.
explanation: Orchestrator-workers is the pattern built for exactly this unpredictability: a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results, which is what's needed when the number and shape of subtasks can't be known until the specific request arrives. The fixed four-stage chain assumes a known, constant decomposition, which breaks the moment a request needs 6 comparison axes instead of 2. Routing only picks one path per request rather than fanning out to a variable number of workers, so it can't handle requests needing several parallel lookups at once. A single long-context agent reading everything linearly forgoes both the parallelism and specialization that make delegation valuable, and doesn't solve the variable-decomposition problem either.
sourceExcerpt: a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results
sourceHighlight: dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs

text: At Vantage Insurance, the claims automation team is building a workflow with three strict stages: first, extract structured data (claimant name, incident date, amount claimed) from an uploaded PDF document; second, validate that extracted data against business rules like coverage limits and policy expiration dates; and third, generate a final adjuster report, but only from data that has already passed validation. Each stage depends entirely on the previous stage's completed output — validation cannot check numbers that haven't been extracted yet, and the report cannot be written from data that hasn't been confirmed valid. An engineer on the team proposed running all three stages concurrently in separate subagents to speed up the pipeline, reasoning that parallel execution is generally faster than sequential execution. The team lead is deciding whether that suggestion is sound given the strict data dependency between stages, or whether a different orchestration pattern is required. Which orchestration pattern fits this workflow, and why is running the stages in parallel not viable here?
options: Parallel execution, since running all three stages concurrently is always faster and dependencies between stages don't actually matter.
An orchestrator-worker pattern with the coordinator guessing likely outputs for stage 2 while stage 1 is still running.
A single subagent handling all three stages with no orchestration needed, since orchestration only matters for parallel work.
A sequential pipeline, because stage 2 cannot run correctly without stage 1's output, and stage 3 cannot run without stage 2's.
explanation: When each stage's input is strictly the previous stage's output, a sequential pipeline is the correct pattern — the dependency chain makes parallel execution not just unhelpful but incorrect, since stage 2 would run on incomplete or absent data. Guessing outputs to unblock parallelism introduces exactly the kind of error the validation stage exists to prevent. Orchestration still matters here even without parallelism, since something still needs to sequence the handoff and pass structured output between stages.
sourceExcerpt: Whereas it's topographically similar, the key difference from parallelization is its flexibility—subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input.
sourceHighlight: subtasks aren't pre-defined, but determined by the orchestrator based on the specific input

text: At Briarcliff Insurance, a coordinator investigating a cluster of suspicious auto-repair claims dispatches three subagents with a single shared instruction: 'look into this claims pattern.' No further breakdown is given to any of them. When the results come back, the fraud analyst notices that two of the three subagents independently spent their entire run pulling the same batch of claimant phone records and flagging the same three claimants, duplicating each other's work almost exactly, while the third subagent wandered off investigating an unrelated agent-licensing compliance issue and never touched the actual pattern of suspiciously similar repair-shop invoices that was the real point of the investigation — a gap the analyst specifically needed covered. This closely mirrors a documented failure mode where a similarly vague instruction caused one subagent to explore an unrelated historical topic while two others duplicated the same current-day research. The team lead now has to redesign how the coordinator dispatches these subagents before the next fraud cluster comes in. What change to the dispatch instructions would most directly fix both the duplication and the coverage gap?
options: Give each subagent a distinct objective, defined output format, and explicit task boundaries, so their coverage areas don't overlap or leave gaps.
Reduce to a single subagent working alone, since assigning more than one subagent inherently causes duplicated investigative effort.
Keep the shared instruction as-is but simply add a fourth subagent to increase the odds that all angles get covered.
Forward the analyst's original one-line request to each subagent unchanged, trusting each to independently infer a distinct angle.
explanation: The documented failure happened for the same reason Briarcliff's did: without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. Giving each subagent its own objective, output format, and clear task boundaries is what prevents both duplication and blind spots. Cutting to a single subagent throws away the coverage and speed benefits of delegation entirely rather than fixing the actual defect, which is vague scoping, not the presence of multiple agents. Adding a fourth subagent without fixing the instruction just adds another agent likely to duplicate or wander, since the shared vague prompt is the root cause. Forwarding the same unchanged one-liner to every subagent is precisely the behavior that produced the overlap and gap in the first place.
sourceExcerpt: one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains
sourceHighlight: 2 others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains

text: At Graystone Legal, a coordinator agent dispatches a discovery-review subagent to sift through several thousand pages of opposing-counsel emails for an active litigation matter, looking for anything relevant to a specific contract dispute. A junior associate reviewing the design assumes the subagent will need to paste large chunks of the raw email text back into the coordinator's own conversation, so the coordinator can 'see' the actual source material directly — the associate is worried that if the subagent instead hands back only a condensed summary, important details buried in the emails will be lost before anyone at the firm gets to see them. Senior counsel pushes back, explaining that the subagent is designed to work through all of the raw material entirely inside its own separate context window, and should return only its distilled findings — not the underlying raw text — to the coordinator. What should actually happen at the handoff between the discovery-review subagent and the coordinator?
options: The subagent should paste as much raw source material as possible back to the coordinator so nothing is lost in the summary.
The subagent works through the raw material entirely within its own context, then returns only its findings to the coordinator, not the raw source.
The subagent and coordinator should share one combined context window so both see every email as it's read.
The subagent should skip reading the actual emails and instead ask the coordinator to summarize the matter for it directly.
explanation: Each subagent independently performs its work and returns findings to the coordinator, distilling potentially enormous raw material down to what actually matters — this compression is a core benefit of subagents operating in their own separate context window rather than flooding the coordinator with everything they touched. Pasting raw source material back defeats that purpose and reintroduces the exact context bloat delegation is meant to avoid. Sharing one combined context window eliminates the isolation that makes a subagent's compression possible in the first place. Having the subagent skip its own investigation and lean on the coordinator inverts the delegation relationship entirely — the coordinator delegated the raw-material review precisely because it didn't want to do that work itself.
sourceExcerpt: Each Subagent independently performs web searches...and returns findings to the LeadResearcher
sourceHighlight: returns findings to the LeadResearcher

text: At Pinehollow Health, a product team is building a patient-facing feature that answers a single factual question per request by pulling from an internal knowledge base — for example, 'what is the copay for a specialist visit under this plan.' Each request is a one-shot lookup: there's no multi-step reasoning, no follow-up action to take, and no ambiguity about what 'done' looks like. One engineer proposes building this as a full autonomous agent with its own planning loop, the ability to call multiple tools across several turns, and the authority to take follow-up actions on its own, arguing that an agentic architecture is inherently more capable and therefore the safer, more future-proof choice. A second engineer pushes back, pointing out that the task as specified is a single well-defined lookup with no multi-step reasoning or environment interaction required, and that layering autonomy on top of it would only add latency, cost, and a new class of failure modes without adding any capability the task actually needs. Which architecture is the better fit here?
options: Agentic architecture, since agents are strictly more capable than single calls, so more autonomy is always the safer default choice.
Agentic architecture, since even simple factual lookups benefit from an agent's ability to pause for human feedback at checkpoints.
An orchestrator-workers pattern, since dynamically delegating the single lookup to a specialized worker best matches the task's real needs.
A single optimized LLM call with retrieval and in-context examples, since that is usually enough for a well-defined, single-step lookup like this.
explanation: For many applications, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough, and a one-shot copay lookup is exactly that kind of well-defined, single-step task — it needs no autonomous planning loop. Treating agents as strictly more capable ignores the real tradeoff: agents' autonomy means higher cost and the potential for compounding errors, which is added risk with no corresponding benefit here since there's no multi-step reasoning to justify it. Human-feedback checkpoints matter for high-stakes multi-step actions, not a single deterministic factual answer. An orchestrator-workers pattern exists to parallelize genuinely independent subtasks, but there's only one subtask here, so there's nothing to decompose or delegate.
sourceExcerpt: For many applications, however, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough
sourceHighlight: optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough

text: A team at Amberlynn Robotics is building an agent that drafts safety-inspection reports for warehouse robots after each maintenance cycle. The first-draft quality coming out of a single generation pass is inconsistent — reports sometimes omit required checklist items like arm-joint torque readings or emergency-stop response times — so the team wants a design where a separate step reviews each draft specifically against the full checklist, sends it back with concrete feedback on exactly what's missing or wrong, and this review-and-revise cycle repeats until a draft actually satisfies every checklist item, rather than the system simply trusting whatever the first draft happens to produce. One engineer argues this is really the orchestrator-workers pattern, since the checklist could be split into sections and assigned to separate specialized workers running at the same time. Another disagrees, pointing out that nothing here is being split into independent parallel sections — it's one draft being repeatedly critiqued and revised until it passes. Which pattern actually matches what Amberlynn needs?
options: An evaluator-optimizer pattern, where one LLM call generates the draft while a separate call evaluates it and feeds back critique in a loop.
An orchestrator-workers pattern, where a central agent decomposes the checklist into independent sections handled by separate specialized worker agents.
A routing pattern, where a classifier decides which single specialized report-writing path a given robot inspection should follow.
A prompt-chaining pattern, where the draft, review, and revision are three fixed steps executed exactly once each in sequence with no repeats.
explanation: This is evaluator-optimizer: one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop, repeating until the output clears the bar — exactly the repeated draft-critique-revise cycle Amberlynn needs given first-draft quality is unreliable. Orchestrator-workers is for decomposing a task into independent parts handled in parallel, but nothing here is being split into separate concurrent sections — it's one draft being iteratively refined. Routing dispatches an input to one of several alternative specialized paths; there's no branching decision being made about which path to take. Prompt chaining runs each fixed step exactly once, which is precisely what does not fit Amberlynn's requirement of repeating review-and-revise until the checklist is actually satisfied.
sourceExcerpt: one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback in a loop
sourceHighlight: evaluation and feedback in a loop

text: Kestrel Freight Analytics runs an agent that monitors shipment exceptions in real time and is authorized to auto-rebook minor delays on its own, without waiting for anyone's approval, since those reroutes are low-stakes and reversible. For one specific class of shipment, however — freight with a declared value over $250,000 — a reroute decision can trigger downstream customs and cargo-insurance implications that are expensive and difficult to unwind if the agent gets it wrong. The operations team wants the agent to keep handling ordinary exceptions fully autonomously, but for this high-value shipment class specifically, they want it to stop short of executing a reroute and instead wait for a human logistics manager's explicit sign-off before the reroute actually goes through, rather than completing the action end-to-end on its own. What is the correct way for the agent to handle a reroute decision on one of these high-value shipments?
options: The agent should always act with full autonomy on every shipment class to maximize response speed, since pausing anywhere slows resolution time.
The agent should silently downgrade the declared value in its own reasoning so the shipment no longer triggers the higher-stakes reroute path.
The agent should pause and wait for human feedback at that checkpoint before executing the high-value reroute, then proceed once approved.
The agent should cancel the high-value shipment's exception handling entirely rather than involve a human reviewer in a reroute decision at all.
explanation: Agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers, and a high-value reroute with customs and insurance implications is exactly the kind of high-stakes action that warrants that checkpoint rather than full autonomy straight through. Always acting with full autonomy ignores that the whole point of a checkpoint is to catch the cases where the cost of an autonomous mistake is high enough to warrant a pause. Having the agent quietly reinterpret or downgrade the declared value to dodge the checkpoint doesn't resolve the risk, it hides it, and isn't a legitimate design response. Simply refusing to handle the exception at all abandons the shipment rather than routing it to the right decision-maker.
sourceExcerpt: Agents can then pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers
sourceHighlight: pause for human feedback at checkpoints

text: An engineer at Cinderglass Data wants a hard guarantee that no pipeline job can ever write to the production dataset without first passing a schema-validation check. While designing the enforcement mechanism, the engineer considers attaching a PostToolUse hook to the write_dataset tool, reasoning that since the hook can inspect the same tool arguments and the result of the call, it should be just as capable of catching and stopping a bad write as a hook running before the call would be. A colleague reviewing the design is skeptical that a PostToolUse hook is the right tool for a guarantee framed as 'never let an unvalidated write happen,' as opposed to a guarantee framed as 'always notice afterward that an unvalidated write happened.' Is attaching a PostToolUse hook to write_dataset actually sufficient to guarantee unvalidated writes never reach the production dataset in the first place?
options: Yes, since a PostToolUse hook can inspect the same arguments a PreToolUse hook would see and stop the write just as effectively.
No, because PostToolUse fires after the tool call already succeeded, so the write has already happened by the time the hook runs.
Yes, since exit code 2 from a PostToolUse hook rolls back the write_dataset call automatically before it reaches the dataset.
No, because PostToolUse hooks cannot read the tool's arguments at all, only its final logged output after the session ends.
explanation: PostToolUse fires after a tool call succeeds, and per the exit-code behavior table, a PostToolUse hook showing stderr to Claude does not undo anything, because the tool already ran — so it cannot prevent an unwanted write to production, only react to one that already happened. Claiming it can stop the write confuses PostToolUse with PreToolUse, which fires beforehand and can actually block the call. Exit code 2 from PostToolUse doesn't roll anything back; there's no automatic undo mechanism described for tool side effects. PostToolUse hooks do receive the tool's arguments and result, so the claim that they can't read arguments at all is also false — the real limitation is timing, not visibility.
sourceExcerpt: PostToolUse | No | Shows stderr to Claude; the tool already ran
sourceHighlight: the tool already ran

text: Quillfeather Retail's inventory agent checks warehouse stock levels throughout a shift by repeatedly calling a warehouse-status API to decide when to trigger restock orders. Each call returns a JSON object with more than 40 fields -- SKU, warehouse zone, aisle, forklift ID, humidity sensor reading, last audit timestamp, pallet weight, and more -- of which the agent's restock task only ever uses three: SKU, current quantity, and restock ETA. The agent's tool-call wrapper appends each full raw response to the conversation as-is. Over a single eight-hour shift the agent makes roughly 25 such calls, and by the last few checks of the shift it starts recommending restock orders for SKUs that were actually replenished hours earlier, or missing ones that are now genuinely low. An engineer confirms the warehouse-status API itself is returning accurate data every time, and the agent's restock-decision logic hasn't changed since the shift began. What is the most likely reason the agent's recommendations degrade over the shift, and what should change?
options: Reduce the number of restock checks performed per shift so fewer tool calls accumulate, even though this means checking fewer SKUs overall.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the full 40-field payloads from all 25 calls can fit without issue.
Trim every tool response down to only the fields the task needs (SKU, quantity, restock ETA) before appending it to context, instead of retaining the full raw payload from each call.
Ask the model to summarize the full history once at the very end of the shift, after all 25 raw responses have already accumulated.
explanation: Every tool result appended to the conversation counts toward the context window, exactly like the system prompt and every other message -- and 25 full 40-plus-field responses accumulate into a large volume of mostly irrelevant data (humidity readings, forklift IDs, audit timestamps) that the model still has to weigh when reasoning about the three fields that actually matter. Trimming each response down to just SKU, quantity, and restock ETA before it enters context keeps that volume from ballooning call after call. Reducing the number of checks sacrifices coverage instead of fixing what's kept from each check. A bigger context window lets all the irrelevant fields keep accumulating instead of addressing why they're there. Summarizing only once at the very end is too late -- by then all 25 raw, mostly-irrelevant responses have already crowded out the specific figures the agent needed throughout the shift.
sourceExcerpt: Everything in the request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, every message in messages (including tool results, images, and documents), and your tool definitions.
sourceHighlight: including tool results, images, and documents

text: Ferrovia Systems has engineers running a multi-agent codebase exploration job to map dependencies across a decade-old monorepo ahead of a planned migration. Several specialized agents crawl different subsystems in parallel, and the whole job is expected to take about six hours. Three hours in, the host machine loses power and the entire session dies mid-exploration. When the on-call engineer restarts the job the next morning, the team wants the coordinator to pick up roughly where it left off rather than re-crawling subsystems that were already fully mapped, since redoing that work would blow the migration deadline. They're debating a few different recovery approaches before committing to one for future long-running jobs. What design would most reliably let the coordinator resume without re-exploring everything from scratch?
options: Restart the entire codebase exploration from the very beginning every single time, since full re-exploration always guarantees fresh and fully accurate findings.
Rely on --resume alone with no additional structured state at all, since resuming a named session automatically restores absolutely everything that was needed.
Keep all accumulated state only inside the crashed process's own memory, and manually retype every single finding by hand once the session fully restarts.
Have each agent export its state to a structured location as it works, and have the coordinator load a manifest of that state on resume, injecting it into the new session.
explanation: Structured state persistence — each agent exporting findings to a known location, with the coordinator loading a manifest of that state on resume — is the reliable pattern for crash recovery, since it survives the crash independent of any single process's memory. Full re-exploration is exactly the wasted, repeated work this design avoids. Session resumption alone helps when prior context is still valid but doesn't substitute for structured state when the session itself crashed. Manually retyping findings is not a reliable or scalable recovery mechanism.

text: You're several hours into a long Claude Code session investigating a gnarly production bug, and you've explored a dozen files, run several failing test suites, and printed verbose stack traces along the way. The context window is now filling up fast with that exploration output, but the key findings you've accumulated — which function is at fault and why — are still accurate and you don't want to lose them. You know that if the context fills completely, either the session will start truncating older messages unpredictably or you'll have to stop and re-derive everything from scratch. You want a way to reclaim context budget right now, in the middle of this same session, without discarding the findings you've already confirmed. What's the appropriate way to reclaim context budget without losing that work?
options: Use /compact to summarize the conversation so far on the server, freeing context space while preserving the important information.
Start an entirely new session with no summary at all, since a clean context is always more reliable than a compacted one.
Manually delete the oldest half of all the messages in the session, regardless of what information they actually contain.
Keep working in the exact same session and simply let the context window overflow silently without intervening at all.
explanation: /compact is designed for exactly this situation: it frees up context space by summarizing the conversation so far, letting you continue without losing important information — preferable to a full restart when the accumulated findings are still valid and worth preserving. Starting completely fresh with nothing carried over throws away accurate, still-relevant work. Deleting the oldest messages indiscriminately risks removing important findings rather than compressible detail. Letting the window overflow risks losing content non-deliberately rather than compressing it deliberately.

text: Support engineers at Solace Freight built an agent that calls an internal order-lookup API to help resolve refund tickets. Each call returns a JSON payload with more than 40 fields — shipping carrier metadata, warehouse routing codes, internal SKU history, and so on — even though the refund-processing task the agent performs only ever needs the order total, refund status, payment method, customer ID, and order date. Over the course of a single shift handling a dozen tickets, these bulky tool results accumulate in the conversation and start crowding out the earlier parts of the case history the agent still needs to reference, occasionally causing it to lose track of details from earlier in the session. The engineering team is evaluating how to stop this accumulation from degrading the agent's performance. What is the most effective fix?
options: Increase the model's context window so all 40+ fields always fit regardless of their relevance.
Trim each tool result to only the fields relevant to the current task before it's added to context.
Stop calling the order-lookup tool altogether, in order to avoid the accumulation problem entirely.
Summarize the entire conversation again after every single tool call, in order to keep it short.
explanation: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, making it important to curate what's actually in context rather than just how much space is available — trimming verbose tool output down to the fields the task actually needs directly reduces irrelevant accumulation without losing needed information. A bigger context window doesn't fix the signal-to-noise problem, it just delays it. Not calling the tool removes needed information along with the noise. Summarizing after every call is far more aggressive and costly than simply filtering fields at the source.
sourceExcerpt: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. This makes curating what's in context just as important as how much space is available.
