text: A financial-services company runs an automated invoice-extraction pipeline that processes about 50,000 documents a day, but only has enough human-reviewer capacity to manually check roughly 500 of them. The team's current approach sends whichever documents happen to be uploaded first each morning, and reviewers keep finding that most of what they check was already correct while genuinely wrong extractions from oddly formatted or low-confidence documents slip through unreviewed. Leadership wants to redesign the routing logic so the limited reviewer hours are spent on the extractions most likely to actually be wrong, using the confidence scores and document metadata the extraction model already produces. Which routing strategy best uses that capacity?
options: Route a fixed random five percent sample of every single extraction straight to human review, regardless of its confidence level or actual content.
Route only the extractions that the model itself explicitly flags as low-confidence in its own free-text commentary field, using no other signal at all.
Route extractions based on field-level confidence scores, document characteristics, and detected field-level ambiguity, prioritizing the cases most likely to be wrong.
Route extractions strictly in alphabetical order by document file name until the reviewer capacity available for that particular day is fully exhausted.
explanation: Confidence- and characteristic-based routing directs limited reviewer attention to the cases most likely to contain errors — ambiguous fields, unusual document types, low model confidence — rather than spending that capacity uniformly. Pure random sampling is useful for measuring aggregate error rates but wastes reviewer time on cases the model already handles reliably. Relying solely on unstructured free-text self-reported confidence is a much weaker and less calibrated signal than field-level confidence scores. Alphabetical routing has no relationship to actual error likelihood at all.
sourceExcerpt: Claude responds well to clear, explicit instructions. Being specific about your desired output can help enhance results.
sourceHighlight: Being specific about your desired output can help enhance results

text: Ledger Point, an invoice-processing vendor, built an extraction pipeline that pulls line items, totals, and vendor IDs from scanned invoices across dozens of document templates. When the pipeline reported 97% overall extraction accuracy in its quarterly dashboard, the operations team decided that figure was high enough to stop routing high-confidence extractions to human reviewers entirely, in order to cut review costs. Eight months later, a client audit reveals that one specific invoice template — used by a mid-size subset of vendors — had actually been failing at nearly a 40% error rate the entire time, silently offset in the dashboard by near-perfect accuracy on the far more common templates. Ledger Point's leadership now wants to know what monitoring practice should have been in place from the start to catch this sooner. What should that have been?
options: Raising the overall accuracy bar required before automating away human review entirely, such as demanding 99% instead of 97%, without changing what gets measured.
A single monthly spot-check of five arbitrary extractions pulled completely at random, regardless of which specific document type or field they represent.
Removing human review from the pipeline entirely the very first time the overall aggregate accuracy score happens to cross a fixed threshold like 95%.
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, broken out by document type and field, to detect novel error patterns hidden inside an aggregate metric.
explanation: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields, so ongoing stratified sampling — deliberately measuring error rates broken out by segment — is what surfaces a silently-failing document type that a single overall percentage would hide. A stricter overall threshold doesn't fix the aggregation problem; a bad segment could still be masked by good segments even at 99%. An arbitrary unstratified spot-check has no guarantee of ever touching the failing document type. Removing review entirely removes the only signal that could have caught the failure. This is the same underlying idea as Claude Code's own guidance to never just trust that work 'looks done' -- give the system a real, structured check rather than a single aggregate signal.
sourceLabel: Claude Code Docs: Best Practices (Give Claude a way to verify its work)
sourceExcerpt: Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare. It's the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from.
sourceHighlight: Give Claude a check it can run

text: During a routine audit, an analyst notices that an extraction tool pulled a contract's total payment amount as $48,000 from page 2 but as $52,000 from page 9 of the same source PDF — the document itself contains two different numbers for what should be a single field, not a case where the model was simply uncertain about a clearly stated value. The extraction pipeline has to decide what to do with this field before the record is marked complete. The team wants a rule that will hold up even when the underlying source, not the model, is the actual origin of the ambiguity. How should this case be routed?
options: Route the extraction to human review, since the ambiguity originates in the source document itself, not in model uncertainty about a clear document.
Have the model silently pick whichever conflicting value happens to appear first on the page and proceed without flagging the discrepancy at all.
Discard the conflicting field entirely and mark the overall record as a successfully completed extraction with a null value inserted in its place.
Automatically average the two conflicting numeric values found across the different pages and simply use that computed result as the final answer.
explanation: Ambiguous or contradictory source documents are exactly the kind of case that should route to human review rather than being resolved silently, since no amount of model confidence calibration fixes a genuinely contradictory source. Silently picking the first value, or averaging the two, both fabricate a resolution the source doesn't actually support. Marking it null without flagging the underlying contradiction discards information a reviewer would need to resolve the conflict correctly. The general principle -- don't let an automated system silently paper over something it can't actually verify -- is the same one behind Claude Code's own recommendation to always provide a real verification signal rather than trust that output 'looks done.'
sourceLabel: Claude Code Docs: Best Practices (Avoid common failure patterns)
sourceExcerpt: The trust-then-verify gap. Claude produces a plausible-looking implementation that doesn't handle edge cases. Fix: Always provide verification (tests, scripts, screenshots). If you can't verify it, don't ship it.
sourceHighlight: If you can't verify it, don't ship it

text: A logistics company's document-extraction model outputs a confidence score between 0 and 1 for every field it pulls, and the team wants to set a threshold below which a field automatically routes to human review. So far, the threshold has just been picked based on what felt reasonable, and nobody has checked whether a field scored at 0.75 is actually wrong more often than one scored at 0.95. The team does have a set of a few thousand historical extractions where humans already verified the correct values, which could be compared against the model's original confidence scores. Before finalizing the threshold company-wide, they want to make sure it's grounded in how the confidence score actually relates to real error rates rather than in a guess. What's the correct way to calibrate that threshold?
options: Pick a round-number threshold like 0.8 purely on gut intuition and apply that single fixed cutoff uniformly across every field and document type regardless.
Use a labeled validation set to measure actual error rates at different confidence levels, and calibrate the review threshold against that measured relationship.
Skip calibration entirely and route every single extraction that scores anything at all below a perfect 1.0 confidence straight to human review.
Ask the model itself what confidence threshold it thinks is appropriate for each field and simply adopt that self-reported value directly without further checking.
explanation: A model's raw confidence score isn't inherently meaningful until it's calibrated against measured outcomes — a labeled validation set lets you determine, empirically, what error rate actually corresponds to a given confidence level, and set the review threshold accordingly. An intuition-based round number has no empirical grounding and may not match the model's real error distribution. Routing everything below 1.0 would send nearly all extractions to review, defeating the purpose of confidence-based triage. Asking the model to self-select its own threshold has the same self-assessment weakness Claude Code's own docs warn about: a fresh, independent check is what catches what self-assessment misses, not the model grading itself.
sourceLabel: Claude Code Docs: Best Practices (Give Claude a way to verify its work)
sourceExcerpt: By a second opinion: a verification subagent or a dynamic workflow that checks its own findings has a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it.
sourceHighlight: so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it

text: Palisade Logistics wants to generate a driver-safety debrief summary for every one of the roughly 2,000 delivery routes completed each day, using trip telemetry and incident logs as input. The summaries only need to be sitting in a dashboard by the time dispatch managers arrive the next morning — nobody is waiting on any individual route's summary as it's generated, and the job runs the same way every single night indefinitely. At 2,000 calls a night, the finance team has flagged the projected annual API spend as a concern and asked engineering to bring the cost down without changing what the dashboard shows. The engineering team is deciding how to structure these nightly calls, and wants a way to identify and resubmit only the handful of routes that fail on a given night rather than rerunning the whole batch. Which approach best fits the requirements, and why?
options: The synchronous Messages API, issuing all 2,000 calls back-to-back in a single sequential loop, since sequential synchronous calls guarantee the lowest per-call latency.
The synchronous Messages API, firing all 2,000 requests concurrently across a large connection pool purely to minimize total wall-clock time for the overnight run.
A single synchronous call that concatenates all 2,000 routes' telemetry into one giant prompt, to avoid the overhead of making thousands of separate API requests entirely.

The Message Batches API, submitting all 2,000 requests with distinct custom_id values so any failed items can be identified and resubmitted, taking advantage of the batch cost discount for this non-blocking overnight workload.
explanation: The Message Batches API is built for exactly this profile: high-volume, non-blocking, cost-sensitive, recurring nightly work, and it offers roughly a 50% cost reduction over synchronous calls for that pattern. Assigning a distinct custom_id to each of the 2,000 requests lets the team match responses back to routes and identify precisely which ones failed, so only those need resubmitting rather than the entire night's batch. Sequential synchronous calls and concurrently-fired synchronous calls both pay full synchronous pricing for a workload that has no latency requirement at all, wasting the cost savings available. Concatenating all 2,000 routes into a single giant prompt doesn't produce 2,000 independent per-route summaries and isn't a workable substitute for per-item processing at this volume.
sourceExcerpt: This approach is well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses, with most batches finishing in less than 1 hour while reducing costs by 50% and increasing throughput.
sourceHighlight: reducing costs by 50%

text: A data team owns a nightly analysis report that the business has come to rely on, and has committed to a 30-hour SLA measured from when the underlying data lands to when the report must be ready. They've moved the report's generation onto the Message Batches API to take advantage of its cost discount, but they know that a batch can take up to 24 hours to complete and there's no guaranteed faster turnaround. Their current process submits exactly one batch each morning at a fixed time, and everyone is aware that if that particular batch happens to take close to the full 24 hours, there won't be much room left before the 30-hour deadline. The team needs a submission schedule that reliably meets the SLA even in the worst case, without giving up the cost benefits of batch processing. How should you schedule submissions to reliably meet the SLA?
options: Submit exactly one batch per day at a single fixed time each morning and simply hope that the 24-hour processing ceiling happens to leave enough margin for the SLA.
Submit as many redundant, overlapping batches as possible all at once simultaneously, on the mistaken assumption that at least one of them is bound to finish quickly.
Switch away from batch processing to the synchronous API entirely, on the mistaken assumption that only fully synchronous calls can ever reliably guarantee any SLA at all.
Submit batches on a schedule with enough buffer below the 24-hour ceiling — e.g., every few hours — so that even a worst-case processing time still lands within the 30-hour SLA window.
explanation: Since batch processing has no guaranteed latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours, meeting a 30-hour end-to-end SLA requires submitting on a schedule with enough buffer that even a worst-case 24-hour batch still completes with room to spare — a single fixed daily submission leaves no margin if that particular batch runs long. Submitting many redundant overlapping batches wastes cost without improving the guarantee, since any individual batch can still take up to 24 hours. Abandoning batch processing for the synchronous API throws away the cost savings that make batch processing worthwhile for a latency-tolerant workload like this.
sourceExcerpt: The Message Batches API is a powerful, cost-effective way to asynchronously process large volumes of Messages requests. This approach is well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses, with most batches finishing in less than 1 hour while reducing costs by 50%.

text: A data engineering team at a legal-tech startup runs a nightly batch job that sends 2,000 document-extraction requests through the Message Batches API, each tagged with a unique custom_id tied to its source document. When the batch completes, the results dashboard shows 1,970 successes and 30 failures — a handful because certain scanned contracts exceeded the model's context window, and the rest due to transient network-level errors during processing. The on-call engineer wants to close out the batch before the morning stand-up without re-paying for the 1,970 requests that already succeeded, and without silently losing the 30 that didn't. She has the full results file in hand, which lists a response or error for every custom_id in the original request set. Given that the team needs both correctness and cost efficiency, what is the correct way to handle the 30 failed requests?
options: Identify the 30 failed requests by their custom_id, apply targeted fixes (e.g., chunking oversized documents), and resubmit only those.
Resubmit the entire original 2,000-request batch again from scratch, just to be extra cautious about any failures that might have been missed.
Discard the 30 failed documents permanently, since a 98.5% aggregate success rate across the batch already looks high enough to simply accept.
Manually reprocess the 30 failures one at a time through the developer console, submitting the exact same unmodified input each time.
explanation: custom_id fields exist to correlate batch request/response pairs, letting you isolate exactly which requests failed and why, then resubmit only those — with modifications like chunking for the ones that failed due to context limits — rather than reprocessing everything. Resubmitting the full 2,000 wastes cost re-running 1,970 requests that already succeeded. Discarding the failures outright silently drops real data rather than fixing the underlying issue. Manually reprocessing with no changes will simply reproduce the same context-limit failures for documents that were too large to begin with.
sourceExcerpt: The Message Batches API is a powerful, cost-effective way to asynchronously process large volumes of Messages requests. This approach is well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses, with most batches finishing in less than 1 hour while reducing costs by 50%.

text: Fennimore Diagnostics runs a medical-imaging triage pipeline where, for every uploaded scan, the model must call a patient_deidentification tool before any of three downstream tools — finding_extraction, severity_scoring, or differential_diagnosis — are allowed to run. During a scale test processing thousands of scans, the team finds that in roughly 1 out of every 15 cases the model calls a downstream analysis tool on its very first turn, before patient_deidentification has run at all, leaving identifying metadata attached to data that later gets logged by the analysis tools. The system prompt already tells the model, in increasingly emphatic language, that deidentification must always come first, but the ordering violations persist. The team needs a fix that structurally guarantees the first tool call in the conversation is patient_deidentification, while still letting the model choose freely among the three analysis tools afterward. What change to the API calls achieves this?
options: Add an even more strongly worded instruction in the system prompt telling the model it must always call deidentification first, before anything else.
Set tool_choice to 'auto' on every single turn so the model retains maximum flexibility to decide the correct calling order entirely by itself.
Force tool_choice to specify the patient_deidentification tool by name for the first turn, then allow free choice among the analysis tools on subsequent turns.
Combine patient_deidentification and all three analysis tools into one single mega-tool, so that call ordering no longer matters at all.
explanation: Forcing a specific named tool via tool_choice guarantees that exact tool is called on that turn, which is the reliable way to enforce a required first step before allowing other tools in later turns. A prompt-level instruction is probabilistic — it is the exact failure mode already described, since the model ignores it in roughly 1 of 15 cases. tool_choice: 'auto' is precisely what allows the out-of-order behavior in the first place, since the model retains free choice on every turn. Merging all four tools into one removes the composability the pipeline needs elsewhere, since severity_scoring and differential_diagnosis still need to run selectively, and doesn't actually resolve sequencing so much as sidestep the tool architecture entirely.
sourceExcerpt: `tool` forces Claude to always use a particular tool.
sourceHighlight: forces Claude to always use a particular tool

text: A fintech company's document-intake pipeline receives scanned PDFs that could be an invoice, a bank statement, a tax form, or a loan application, and a separate extraction tool with its own schema exists for each document type. In production, the team found that when a scanned PDF is unusually noisy or ambiguous, the model sometimes replies with a plain conversational sentence like "I'm not entirely sure which document type this is" instead of calling any extraction tool, which breaks the downstream parser that expects a structured tool call on every request. The document type genuinely cannot be known in advance by the pipeline itself — only the model, after reading the content, can determine which schema applies. Engineering wants a configuration that forces the model to call one of the four extraction tools on every request, without hardcoding which one in advance, so that plain-text fallback responses become impossible. Which tool_choice configuration satisfies this requirement?
options: tool_choice: "auto", since it gives the model complete discretion to decide for itself what response is best in this situation.
tool_choice forced to one single specific tool name in advance, even though the actual document type is genuinely unknown ahead of time.
tool_choice: {"type": "any"}, since it forces the model to call some tool while still letting it pick which one fits the document.
No tool_choice configuration at all, relying entirely on the system prompt's wording to request that some tool gets used.
explanation: tool_choice: {"type": "any"} guarantees the model calls one of the available tools rather than returning conversational text, while still letting it select which tool matches the actual document type — exactly the flexibility this ambiguous-type scenario needs. "auto" permits a plain-text response, which is the failure mode the pipeline can't tolerate. Forcing one specific tool name is wrong when the document type is genuinely unknown in advance and might not match that tool at all. Omitting tool_choice and hoping the system prompt is enough reintroduces the same unreliability "any" is designed to eliminate.
sourceExcerpt: Setting strict: true on a tool definition guarantees Claude’s tool inputs match your JSON Schema. Combining tool_choice: {"type": "any"} with strict tool use guarantees both that one of your tools will be called AND that the tool inputs strictly follow your schema.
sourceHighlight: guarantees both that one of your tools will be called AND that the tool inputs strictly follow your schema

text: A platform engineering team built an automated code-review bot that classifies every finding as critical, major, or minor, with each severity level defined only in prose inside the system prompt. After running the bot across several dozen pull requests, reviewers notice that a null-pointer-dereference-style bug is labeled "critical" in one file and "minor" in a nearly identical file elsewhere in the same repo, and the inconsistency is eroding the team's trust in the bot's triage. The prompt already goes into real depth about what distinguishes each severity tier, so simply repeating or rephrasing those descriptions hasn't helped. The team wants findings from the same underlying bug class to receive the same severity label consistently, without discarding the severity distinction developers rely on to prioritize fixes. What change to the prompt would most effectively fix the inconsistency?
options: Remove severity levels entirely from the prompt and simply report every single finding at the exact same flat priority level.
Instruct the model to simply "use your best judgment" about severity without providing any further detail or examples.
Increase the number of prose adjectives used to describe each severity level, such as "very critical" versus "extremely critical".
Add few-shot examples pairing concrete code snippets with their correct severity label and a short rationale for each level.
explanation: Few-shot examples pairing real code with the correct severity label and rationale give the model concrete anchors for a judgment call that prose definitions alone leave too open to interpretation, directly targeting consistency across similar cases. Removing severity entirely discards useful information rather than fixing the inconsistency. Telling the model to use its best judgment is the same underspecified instruction already producing inconsistent results. Piling on more prose adjectives doesn't supply the concrete grounding examples provide.
sourceExcerpt: Few well-crafted examples (known as few-shot or multishot prompting) improve accuracy and consistency. Effective examples should be relevant (mirroring your actual use case closely) and diverse (covering edge cases).
sourceHighlight: improve accuracy and consistency

text: Brackenfield Freight's infrastructure team is preparing a linting pass across a large monorepo containing thousands of files spanning application code, scripts, and infrastructure config. Before running the linter, an engineer needs to compile the complete list of every Terraform file that matches the **/*.tf naming convention anywhere in the repository, regardless of which subdirectory it lives in. She isn't interested yet in what any of these files actually contain -- only in the full set of matching file paths, gathered as quickly as possible, so the linter can be pointed at exactly the right files. Opening and reading every file in the repository just to check its extension would be enormously wasteful for a task that's really about names, not content, and she'd rather reach for a purpose-built tool than write a custom shell script. Which built-in tool is the right choice for this file-discovery task?
options: Glob, since it matches files by name/path pattern rather than by content.
Grep, since it can search file contents across the entire repository at once.
Read, since the file contents must be inspected to confirm each match.
Bash, since only a hand-written shell command can perform this kind of pattern search.
explanation: Glob is purpose-built for finding files by name or path pattern, which is exactly what's needed here since the task is entirely about which files exist under a naming convention, not what they contain. Grep searches file contents for patterns like text or function names, which isn't relevant when no content matching is required. Read loads and returns full file contents, which would be wasteful and unnecessary just to confirm a file's extension. Reaching for Bash and a hand-written find-style command works in principle, but it duplicates functionality the built-in Glob tool already provides more directly, without any real benefit.

text: Bluewater Diagnostics configures a new code-review subagent and wants to restrict it to a read-only investigative role: it should be able to read files and search file contents, but must never edit files, run shell commands, or write anything. An engineer writes the subagent's tools list as read, grep in its configuration, expecting this to grant exactly Read and Grep access and nothing else. After deploying the subagent, the team notices it behaves as though it has no tool access at all -- it describes what it would look for but never actually opens or searches any file, even for straightforward lookups it should easily be able to perform. Reviewing the platform's tools documentation, the team wants to understand why the restriction silently failed to grant the intended access instead of just narrowing it as expected. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The subagent's tools list has a maximum of one entry, so listing two tool names caused the entire list to be ignored.
Tool names in configuration lists must match the exact strings Claude Code uses internally, and lowercase read, grep don't match the actual tool names Read and Grep.
Read-only subagents are not permitted to call any tools at all, regardless of what is listed in their configuration.
The configuration file needs to be reloaded manually after every edit, and the team simply hasn't restarted the session yet.
explanation: Claude Code's built-in tools are referenced in configuration by their exact names -- the same strings used in permission rules, subagent tool lists, and hook matchers. The actual tool names are Read and Grep, capitalized exactly that way; lowercase strings like read and grep don't match them, so the intended restriction silently fails to grant any tool access at all rather than narrowing it as expected. There's no rule limiting a tools list to a single entry, so that explanation doesn't hold. Read-only subagents can absolutely be granted specific tools like Read and Grep -- restricting them to zero tools isn't a built-in requirement. And while a stale configuration is a real class of bug, the scenario is a naming mismatch, not a caching issue, since the listed names never matched real tool names in the first place.

text: Amberline Retail is retiring a deprecated pricing function, calculateDiscount, from a codebase with several hundred files built up over many years. Before removing it, an engineer needs to find every caller so nothing breaks. She quickly discovers the function has been re-exported under different names in at least two wrapper modules -- one file re-exports it as computeDiscount, and a legacy checkout module aliases it as legacyPriceAdjust -- so plenty of real call sites never reference the literal string calculateDiscount at all. Her manager warns that grepping only the original name and deleting every match would miss those aliased callers entirely, silently breaking checkout and pricing pages that import the wrapper names instead. She wants an approach that reliably surfaces every real caller, including the aliased ones, without reading the entire repository file by file. What is the most reliable exploration strategy?
options: Grep only for calculateDiscount across the repository, and remove every direct match found, since that is the function's real name.
Use Glob to list every file whose name contains 'discount', and treat that file list as the complete set of callers.

First identify the wrapper and re-export modules and every alias they define, grep for each alias name in addition to the original, then Read the surrounding code at each match to confirm real usage before removing anything.
Ask a fresh agent to reimplement calculateDiscount and its wrapper modules from scratch, rather than tracing the existing callers.

Grepping only the literal name calculateDiscount misses every call site that imports it under an alias like computeDiscount or legacyPriceAdjust, silently breaking those callers. Using Glob to gather files with 'discount' in their name only produces a name-based guess at relevant files; it says nothing about which files actually call the function, and would miss files named anything else. Reimplementing the function from scratch doesn't address the actual task, which is safely removing the existing one after confirming every real caller has been found.

text: An agent connected to a company's issue tracker via MCP is tasked with triaging bugs, but engineers notice it repeatedly issues a "list all open issues" tool call at the start of nearly every task, just to re-orient itself on which issues currently exist, before doing any real work on the specific ticket it was asked about. This repeated listing call adds latency and eats into the agent's available turns before it even starts investigating. The issue catalog changes frequently enough that a static, manually maintained list would go stale within days, and the team also doesn't want to rely on the agent's own memory carrying over between sessions, since that isn't reliable. The team wants the current catalog of open issues available to the agent as reference content it can consult directly, without repeatedly invoking an action-style tool call just to see what's there. How should this issue catalog be exposed to the agent to cut down on the redundant listing calls?
options: As an MCP tool that the agent must explicitly call every single time it needs to check which open issues currently exist in the tracker.
As a hardcoded list baked into the system prompt, manually updated by a person each time an issue gets newly opened or closed.
By instructing the agent to cache its own memory of the full issue list internally, carrying it over between separate working sessions.
As an MCP resource exposing the issue catalog as content the agent can reference directly, reducing repeated exploratory tool calls.
explanation: MCP resources are meant for exposing content catalogs — like an issue tracker's summaries — as data the agent can reference, which is precisely the mechanism for reducing exploratory tool calls compared to treating the same catalog as an action-oriented tool the agent has to invoke repeatedly. Modeling it purely as a callable tool keeps the exploratory-call overhead the scenario is trying to eliminate. A manually maintained system-prompt list goes stale and doesn't scale. Relying on the agent's own session memory doesn't help across a single session where the repeated calls are already happening, and isn't reliable across agent restarts.
sourceExcerpt: MCP servers give Claude Code access to your tools, databases, and APIs. Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker or a monitoring dashboard.
sourceHighlight: Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat

text: Windmere Analytics is building an agent workflow around a nightly data pipeline. Immediately after a new dataset lands, the agent must call validate_schema before doing anything else with the data -- skipping that check even once has already caused a corrupted report to reach a client. Elsewhere in the same application, analysts chat with the agent about routine questions, and the team wants the model to freely decide for itself whether calling any tool is even necessary for those casual turns. The engineering team is configuring tool_choice separately for each part of the workflow and wants the post-upload validation step, specifically, to guarantee that validate_schema always runs immediately, with no possibility of the model skipping it or calling a different tool instead. Which tool_choice setting should they apply to that specific step?
options: auto, so the model can decide for itself whether calling validate_schema is necessary each time.
any, so the model is required to call some tool, though not necessarily validate_schema.
a forced named tool, pointing tool_choice at validate_schema specifically, so that exact tool always runs.
none, so no tool call happens and validate_schema runs through a separate scheduled job instead.
explanation: Only a forced named tool call guarantees a specific tool executes: it points tool_choice directly at validate_schema, so that exact tool is what runs immediately after upload, with no possibility of the model skipping it or picking something else. auto leaves the decision entirely up to the model, which is appropriate for the casual analyst chat turns elsewhere but doesn't guarantee anything for this step. any forces some tool call but doesn't pin down which one, so the model could technically satisfy it by calling a different tool instead of validate_schema. none prevents any tool call at all, which is the opposite of what's needed immediately after a new dataset lands and must be validated before anything else happens.
sourceExcerpt: `tool` forces Claude to always use a particular tool.
sourceHighlight: forces Claude to always use a particular tool

text: Draycott Software's MCP server exposes a charge_customer tool to its billing agent. Whatever actually goes wrong -- an expired card, insufficient permissions to charge a given account, or a five-second network timeout to the payment processor -- the tool returns the same generic string: 'Operation failed.' In production, the agent responds to every failure the same way: it retries with exponential backoff. For a permission error that will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried, this burns several turns before the agent gives up and escalates anyway. For a genuinely transient timeout that would likely succeed on a second attempt, the agent sometimes gives up and escalates to a human after just one retry, since it has no way to tell the transient case apart from the permanent one. The team wants to redesign the tool's error responses so the agent can behave correctly in both situations. What is the most effective fix?
options: Keep the generic 'Operation failed' message, and apply a fixed exponential-backoff retry policy uniformly to every failure the tool returns.
Keep the generic message returned to the agent, but log full stack traces server-side so engineers can investigate failures later.

Return structured errors that include a category such as transient, validation, or permission, an is_retryable flag, and a specific human-readable cause, so the agent can decide whether and how to retry.
Remove error messages entirely and let failed calls return no output at all, so the agent infers failure only from the absence of an expected result.
explanation: Structured errors that carry a category (transient, validation, permission), an is_retryable flag, and a specific human-readable cause give the agent the signal it needs to behave correctly in each case: retry the timeout, and stop immediately on the permission error instead of burning turns on something that will never succeed. A blanket exponential-backoff policy applied to every failure wastes turns retrying errors, like permission failures, that can never succeed no matter how many attempts are made. Logging full stack traces server-side helps engineers later, but gives the agent in the moment nothing more to act on than the same generic string. Removing error messages and returning no output at all is strictly worse: the agent loses even the coarse signal that something failed, let alone why.
sourceLabel: Anthropic Engineering: Writing Tools for Agents
sourceExcerpt: Tool truncation and error responses can steer agents towards more token-efficient tool-use behaviors.
sourceHighlight: error responses can steer agents towards more token-efficient tool-use behaviors

text: Silvergate Robotics exposes two MCP tools to its fleet-support agent: search_inventory, described only as 'Searches inventory,' and check_warranty_status, described only as 'Checks warranty.' Neither description says what parameters each tool expects, what fields the response contains, or how either tool behaves for edge cases like a part that's out of stock or a serial number with no warranty on file. In practice, the agent frequently calls search_inventory when a customer is actually asking about warranty coverage, and occasionally calls check_warranty_status when the customer is really asking whether a part is in stock. A teammate suggests the fix is architectural -- inserting a keyword-based routing layer in front of both tools to decide which one to call. The support lead disagrees and wants to address the actual cause of the misrouting before adding any new layer. What is most likely to fix the underlying problem?
options: Add a routing agent in front of both tools that picks which one to call based on keywords in the customer's message.
Increase the context window available to the model so it can weigh more prior conversation turns before choosing a tool.
Give both tools punchier, more distinct-sounding names, while leaving their one-line descriptions unchanged.
Rewrite both tools' descriptions to be extremely detailed: what each tool does, when to use it, its expected inputs and outputs, and edge cases like out-of-stock parts or missing warranty records.
explanation: The root cause here is that neither tool's description says what it does beyond a two-word summary, so the model has no reliable way to tell them apart when a request could plausibly match either one; rewriting both descriptions to be extremely detailed -- covering purpose, when to use each tool, expected inputs and outputs, and edge cases -- directly removes that ambiguity. A keyword-based routing layer adds a new component on top of the same underlying problem instead of fixing why the model can't distinguish the tools itself. A larger context window doesn't help the model reason about tool boundaries that are inherently vague, regardless of how much conversation history it can consider. And renaming the tools without improving their descriptions leaves the actual missing information -- what each tool does and when to use it -- exactly as absent as before.
sourceExcerpt: Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance.
sourceHighlight: This is by far the most important factor in tool performance

text: Marrow Health Systems has grown its internal MCP tool library to roughly 30 tools spanning three different backend services: a ticketing system, a team chat platform, and an internal lab-sample database. Many of these tools share the same generic names across services -- there's a search tool for tickets, a search tool for chat messages, and a search tool for lab samples, plus similarly generic create and list tools in each service. As the library has grown, the agent has started calling the wrong service's search tool when a request could plausibly apply to more than one -- searching chat messages for a lab result, for instance, instead of querying the lab database directly. The platform team wants a fix that scales as more services are added later, not a one-off patch for just these three. What should they do?
options: Merge all three services' generic tools into one shared search and one shared list tool, each taking a service parameter to pick the backend.
Prefix each tool with its service and resource, for example lab_search_samples, ticket_search_issues, and chat_send_message, so tool names are unambiguous as the library keeps growing.
Leave the tool names as they are, but add a short disambiguation reminder to the system prompt every time a generic tool name is invoked.
Remove the least-used service's tools from the library entirely instead of renaming anything.
explanation: Prefixing each tool with its service and resource, like lab_search_samples, ticket_search_issues, and chat_send_message, is exactly the recommended fix for a tool library spanning multiple services with generically named tools, and it scales cleanly as more services are added later since new tools simply get their own prefix. Merging the three services' tools into one shared search and list tool with a service parameter conflates genuinely different backends and resource types rather than consolidating overlapping actions on the same resource. Adding a system-prompt reminder patches the symptom for existing tools but doesn't prevent the same ambiguity from recurring with every new service added later. And removing a service's tools entirely doesn't solve an ambiguity problem -- it just deletes functionality the team presumably still needs.
sourceExcerpt: Use meaningful namespacing in tool names. When your tools span multiple services or resources, prefix names with the service (for example, `github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`). This makes tool selection unambiguous as your library grows
sourceHighlight: prefix names with the service

text: Talon Data's list_shipments MCP tool returns, for every shipment, an internal numeric row ID like 88213, a fully nested JSON object with all 50-plus database columns for that row, and no limit on how many shipments a single call can return. For a large customer account, one call to list_shipments has returned over 12,000 rows in a single response, blowing well past the agent's context budget and leaving it very little useful signal to act on amid all the raw data. The row IDs are also meaningless on their own -- an agent that wants to reference 'shipment 88213' later in the conversation has no readable, stable way to do so. The team is redesigning the tool's response shape and wants a fix that addresses both the token bloat and the unhelpful identifiers at once, following the same practices the rest of their tool library already uses elsewhere. What should they do?
options: Switch numeric row IDs to semantic identifiers like shipment slugs or UUIDs, trim each response to only the fields the agent actually needs, and add pagination or truncation with sensible default limits so a single call can't return unbounded results.
Keep returning every field and every row unmodified, but add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent to only look at the fields relevant to its current task.
Leave the field set and row IDs exactly as they are, but attach a warning banner to any response containing more than 5,000 rows.
Replace list_shipments with a raw SQL-execution tool so the agent can write its own queries specifying exactly which fields and row limits it wants.
explanation: Switching to semantic, stable identifiers, trimming responses down to only the fields the agent needs, and adding pagination or truncation with sensible defaults addresses both problems at once: it makes shipment references legible, and it guarantees no single call can flood the agent's context with 12,000 rows of mostly irrelevant data. Instructing the agent via the system prompt to 'only look at the fields it needs' doesn't reduce what's actually sent back or fix the unreadable numeric IDs; the bloat and cryptic identifiers are still there consuming context. A size-based warning banner tells the agent a response was large after the fact, without shrinking it or making the IDs any more meaningful. Replacing the tool with raw SQL access shifts the entire burden of field selection and row limits onto the agent, trading a clear tool interface for a much more error-prone, cryptic one.
sourceLabel: Anthropic Engineering: Writing Tools for Agents
sourceExcerpt: We suggest implementing some combination of pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation with sensible default parameter values.
sourceHighlight: pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation

text: A vendor-hosted MCP server used by the support team at Lumen Cloud regularly adds and removes tools as the vendor ships new features on their own release schedule, entirely outside the support team's control. Historically, whenever the vendor added a new tool, engineers had to manually disconnect and reconnect the server inside Claude Code before the new tool became available, which meant new capabilities often sat unused for days until someone remembered to reconnect. The team wants Claude Code to just pick up these changes automatically going forward. What capability, if the vendor's server supports it, would let Claude Code refresh its available tools without anyone manually disconnecting and reconnecting?
options: Increasing the server's per-tool timeout value so Claude Code polls the server more frequently for configuration changes.
Setting oauth.scopes to a broader value so the server is authorized to advertise additional tools without a reconnect.
The server sending an MCP list_changed notification, which Claude Code uses to automatically refresh its available tools, prompts, and resources.
Enabling the claude/channel capability so the server can push each new tool definition directly into the conversation as a message.
explanation: Claude Code supports MCP list_changed notifications specifically so a server can dynamically update its available tools, prompts, and resources without requiring anyone to disconnect and reconnect -- when the server sends this notification, Claude Code automatically refreshes what it knows is available from that server. A timeout value only bounds how long a tool call is allowed to run, not how tool lists are refreshed. oauth.scopes governs authorization scope, not tool-list discovery. The claude/channel capability is for pushing event-driven messages into a session (like CI results or chat notifications), a different mechanism from updating the tool catalog itself.
sourceExcerpt: Claude Code supports MCP list_changed notifications, allowing MCP servers to dynamically update their available tools, prompts, and resources without requiring you to disconnect and reconnect. When an MCP server sends a list_changed notification, Claude Code automatically refreshes the available capabilities from that server.
sourceHighlight: allowing MCP servers to dynamically update their available tools, prompts, and resources without requiring you to disconnect and reconnect

text: During a flaky network window, two of Meridian Analytics' MCP servers both lose connectivity mid-session: a remote billing-api server reachable over HTTP, and a local local-cache server that Claude Code launched as a stdio subprocess on the developer's own machine. Ten minutes later, the developer notices billing-api silently reconnected on its own, while local-cache is still shown as disconnected and never came back without the developer manually restarting it. Why did only one of the two servers recover automatically?
options: Claude Code automatically reconnects HTTP and SSE servers with exponential backoff after a disconnect, but stdio servers are local processes and are not reconnected automatically.
Both servers should have reconnected automatically; the difference is a bug specific to how local-cache happened to be configured, not a general rule about transports.
Only servers added at user scope ever reconnect automatically, and local-cache was likely added at project or local scope instead.
Automatic reconnection only applies to servers that have completed OAuth authentication, and stdio servers are never able to authenticate via OAuth.
explanation: If an HTTP or SSE server disconnects mid-session, Claude Code automatically reconnects with exponential backoff -- up to five attempts, starting at a one-second delay and doubling each time. Stdio servers, by contrast, are local processes rather than network connections Claude Code can retry against, so they are not reconnected automatically and need a manual restart. This is a transport-level distinction, not a scope-based rule or an OAuth-authentication requirement -- most stdio servers don't use OAuth at all, since those flags only apply to HTTP and SSE transports.
sourceExcerpt: If an HTTP or SSE server disconnects mid-session, Claude Code automatically reconnects with exponential backoff: up to five attempts, starting at a one-second delay and doubling each time. ... Stdio servers are local processes and are not reconnected automatically.
sourceHighlight: Stdio servers are local processes and are not reconnected automatically

text: A get_schema tool on an internal MCP server at Cobalt Freight returns the entire database schema for a large analytics warehouse, often tens of thousands of tokens in a single response. Engineers keep seeing Claude Code's output warning trigger, and responses from this specific tool are frequently persisted to disk and replaced with a file reference instead of being shown inline, which breaks a workflow that depends on reading the schema directly in the conversation. Raising the global MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS environment variable helps a little, but the team wants a fix that specifically targets this one large-but-necessary tool without loosening limits for every other MCP tool in the environment. What is the correct fix?
options: Ask every engineer to individually set MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS to its maximum possible value in their own personal shell configuration.
Have the server set _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] on the get_schema tool's tools/list entry to raise that specific tool's output threshold.
Switch the get_schema tool from HTTP to stdio transport, since stdio servers are exempt from all MCP output size limits entirely.
Mark the tool with _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true so oversized responses are approved manually instead of being persisted to disk.
explanation: The anthropic/maxResultSizeChars annotation lets an individual tool declare its own higher output threshold (up to a hard ceiling of 500,000 characters), which Claude Code honors for that tool's text content independent of whatever MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS is set to globally -- exactly the targeted, per-tool fix this scenario calls for. Raising the global environment variable for every engineer loosens the limit everywhere, not just for this one large-but-necessary tool. Output size limits are a general MCP behavior, not something transport-specific that stdio servers are exempt from. requiresUserInteraction controls whether a tool always needs an explicit approval prompt; it has nothing to do with output size or the persist-to-disk threshold.
sourceExcerpt: If you're building an MCP server, you can allow individual tools to return results larger than the default persist-to-disk threshold by setting _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] in the tool's tools/list response entry. Claude Code raises that tool's threshold to the annotated value, up to a hard ceiling of 500,000 characters.
sourceHighlight: Claude Code raises that tool's threshold to the annotated value, up to a hard ceiling of 500,000 characters

text: A compliance team at Solstice Bank is building an MCP server with a grant_access tool that provisions elevated database permissions for a requesting engineer. Legal has been explicit: this specific action must always be reviewed and explicitly approved by a human on every single call, with no exceptions, even for engineers who run Claude Code in auto or bypassPermissions mode for their day-to-day work, and even if an existing allow rule would otherwise match this tool. The team wants a way to guarantee this at the tool's own definition, rather than hoping every engineer's personal permission configuration happens to be strict enough. How should the server guarantee this?
options: Document the requirement clearly in the tool's description field, instructing Claude never to call it without first confirming with the user.
Set _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true on the tool's tools/list entry so its permission prompt always appears, regardless of mode or allow rules.
Require every engineer to individually configure their own personal settings to deny this tool by name before they are permitted to use the server at all.
Rely on the server rejecting the call server-side unless a specific header is present, since Claude Code's own permission modes cannot be trusted to enforce this.
explanation: Setting _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true on the tool's tools/list entry makes Claude Code show that tool's permission prompt on every call, even in acceptEdits, auto, and bypassPermissions permission modes, without offering a "don't ask again" option -- and allow rules that would otherwise match the tool don't skip the prompt either. This is a server-side, tool-level guarantee rather than something that depends on each engineer's personal configuration being strict enough. A description-field instruction is only a prompt-level suggestion the model could still fail to follow. Requiring every engineer to manually deny the tool by name is fragile and easy to skip. Relying purely on a server-side header check abandons Claude Code's own confirmation mechanism rather than using the annotation built specifically for this case.
sourceExcerpt: If you're building an MCP server, you can mark a tool as requiring explicit approval on every call by setting _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"] to true in the tool's tools/list response entry. ... Claude Code shows that tool's permission prompt on every call, even in acceptEdits, auto, and bypassPermissions permission modes, and doesn't offer a "don't ask again" option for it. Allow rules that match the tool don't skip the prompt either.
sourceHighlight: Claude Code shows that tool's permission prompt on every call, even in acceptEdits, auto, and bypassPermissions permission modes

text: A third-party MCP server connected to Claude Code at Ashgrove Capital defines one of its tools with a JSON Schema input that uses oneOf at the very top level of the schema, since the tool genuinely accepts two structurally different shapes of input depending on the request type. An engineer reviewing the integration recalls reading that the Claude API doesn't accept anyOf, oneOf, or allOf combinators at the root of a tool's input schema, and is confused why the tool still shows up and works correctly in Claude Code rather than failing outright. What is actually happening?
options: Claude Code silently drops the oneOf constraint entirely and accepts any input shape the model happens to produce for that tool.
The MCP server is misconfigured and this tool should not actually be working; the engineer is likely looking at cached results from before the schema was added.
Claude Code flattens the root-level combinator into a single object schema before sending it to the API, and adds a sentence to the tool's description telling Claude which parameters belong together.
Claude API added native support for root-level oneOf schemas, so no special handling is needed on Claude Code's side any longer.
explanation: Claude Code detects a tool schema with a root-level combinator (anyOf, oneOf, or allOf), flattens it into a single object schema the API will accept, and prepends a sentence to the tool's description explaining which parameter groups belong together -- for anyOf/oneOf specifically, each branch's properties are merged and its required list is described in the text rather than enforced by the schema itself, so the server still needs to validate the actual argument combination it receives. Nothing is silently dropped, this isn't a caching artifact, and the Claude API itself still doesn't natively accept root-level combinators -- the rewrite happens entirely on Claude Code's side before the request goes out.
sourceExcerpt: Before sending the tool to the API, Claude Code flattens the schema into a single object and prepends a sentence to the tool's description that tells Claude which parameter groups belong together ... Your server receives whichever arguments Claude chose, so keep validating the combination server-side.
sourceHighlight: Claude Code flattens the schema into a single object and prepends a sentence to the tool's description that tells Claude which parameter groups belong together

text: A team at Ridgeline Software installs a plugin called db-tools-plugin that bundles its own MCP server, registered internally as database-tools, exposing a query tool. When a security engineer writes a hook intended to intercept every call to that tool, she writes the matcher as mcp__database-tools__.*, expecting it to catch calls from the plugin-bundled server the same way it would for a manually-configured server of that name. During testing, the hook never fires, even though the query tool is clearly being called successfully. What is she missing about how plugin-bundled MCP tool names actually work?
options: Plugin-bundled MCP tools cannot be matched by hooks at all under any circumstances, regardless of how the matcher is written.
The tool's callable name actually takes the form mcp__plugin_db-tools-plugin_database-tools__query, embedding the plugin name, so a matcher written against just the bare server key never matches it.
Hook matchers only work against tools from manually-configured servers added via claude mcp add, never against tools from any plugin whatsoever.
The hook is written correctly, but hooks for MCP tools only fire on the very first call to that tool per session, not on every subsequent call.
explanation: Tools from a plugin-bundled MCP server include both the plugin name and the server key in their callable name, in the full form mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool-name>. For the database-tools server bundled in db-tools-plugin, the query tool's real callable name is mcp__plugin_db-tools-plugin_database-tools__query -- a hook matcher written against the bare server key, like mcp__database-tools__.*, never fires for a plugin-bundled server, because that pattern doesn't match the plugin-qualified name the tool actually registers under. Plugin MCP tools absolutely can be matched by hooks, and there's no first-call-only restriction -- the fix is simply writing the matcher against the correct, plugin-qualified tool name.
sourceExcerpt: Tools from a plugin-bundled MCP server include both the plugin name and the server key in their callable name. The full form is mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool-name> ... A hook matcher written against the bare server key, such as mcp__database-tools__.*, never fires for a plugin-bundled server.
sourceHighlight: never fires for a plugin-bundled server

text: An engineer at Coppergate Bank wants to know the moment a nightly reconciliation job fails, rather than remembering to ask Claude to check its status every morning. She assumes MCP servers can only ever respond to requests that Claude sends -- Claude asks, the server answers -- and concludes that a genuinely proactive alert, one that reaches her without her prompting Claude first, simply isn't possible through MCP. Her fallback plan is to set a personal calendar reminder each morning to open Claude Code and ask it to check the job status by hand. Before committing to that manual workaround, she asks a colleague who has built MCP integrations before whether her assumption is actually correct. Is she right that this kind of proactive push is impossible, and if not, what should she use instead?
options: She's right -- MCP connections are strictly request-and-response, so a recurring manual check, or a separate external paging system, is the only way to get notified.
She's right that true pushes aren't possible, but she can approximate one by having Claude poll the job status every few minutes for the rest of the day.
She's wrong -- an MCP server can act as a channel that pushes messages into her session, so Claude can react to a failure event or webhook on its own, without her asking first.
She's wrong, but achieving this means bypassing MCP entirely and building a custom polling loop directly into her system prompt instead.
explanation: MCP isn't limited to responding only when Claude asks first -- a server can also act as a channel that pushes messages into a session, reacting to things like webhook events on its own timeline, which is exactly the mechanism that fits a 'notify me the moment this job fails' requirement. A recurring manual check or a separate external paging system works, but it isn't necessary and misses the fact that MCP itself supports this. Having Claude poll every few minutes still requires her to keep a session open and doesn't actually deliver a push; it's a workaround for a limitation that doesn't really exist here. And building a custom polling loop into the system prompt bypasses a capability MCP already provides, adding complexity for no benefit.
sourceExcerpt: an MCP server can also act as a channel that pushes messages into your session, so Claude reacts to Telegram messages, Discord chats, or webhook events while you're away
sourceHighlight: an MCP server can also act as a channel that pushes messages into your session
